As the title hints, "Batman Begins" is not a sequel to the three (the latest previous attempt doesn't count) recent installments featuring the Caped Crusader, but rather a new dawn that unabashedly ignores any established precedents. The end result is as intended, breathing brilliant new life into a series that had unfortunately become a laughingstock.The script's blueprint invigorates the film. Because of the audience's general familiarity with the title character, "Batman Begins" is able to concentrate on his origin and motivations rather than the crime fighting itself. Like "Superman", the best superhero movie ever, the film spends a significant portion of its running length on the how and why instead of the what. We observe the fears and struggles that Bruce Wayne faces, which simultaneously humanizes him and heightens his mythic status.This course of action is primarily executed over the first ninety minutes, during which a depth beyond the typical perfunctory introduction of motives is established. Batman's fearsome aura, the source of his power in both the fictional world of Gotham and the real world of moviegoers, is detailed, resulting in a movie more fascinating psychological thriller than standard adventure flick, although the action scenes still shine, one Batmobile-charged chase in particular. Eventually of course the inevitable protagonist-antagonist showdown evolves, and then the movie deteriorates slightly, but by that point "Batman Begins" has reached such heights that neither the slight come-down nor occasional cinematic conveniences and niceties (why the kid?) derail the picture.Aiding in the climb to excellence is the best supporting cast of any Batman film, filled with respected and recognizable faces who nail roles as they suitably show more restraint than many in the prior versions. Cillian Murphy is extra creepy as the the shady psychologist Dr. Crane; Liam Neeson authoritative as Ducard, Bruce Wayne's mentor; Gary Oldman, even though you half-expect him to go psycho at any moment, evokes an excellent world-weariness as Detective Gordon; Michael Caine adds strength to the butler Alfred; and Morgan Freeman as Batman's pseudo-Q is...well, has Freeman ever been anything less than superb? Other talented actors like Tom Wilkinson (crime boss Carmine Falcone), Ken Watanabe (the enigmatic Ra's Al Ghul), and Rutger Hauer (the business head of Wayne Enterprises) round out the predominantly male cast interestingly loaded with Brits. As the mandatory female love interest, Mrs. Tom Cruise...er...Katie Holmes, is fully adequate and attractive, although her part could have been played by numerous actresses.All that talent matters little if the man behind the cape and cowl falters. But Christian Bale never wavers in either portion of his role. I'll say it...Bale is better than Keaton, Kilmer, or Clooney, combining the best of the two former actors. As Bruce Wayne, he surpasses Keaton's charming playfulness and Kilmer's suave businessman with a twinkle befitting the younger man. As Batman, Bale possesses a masked intensity that blows away all of them, embodying the tortured soul through menacing facial expressions and a daunting physical presence that none of his predecessors maintained consistently.Beyond an omnipresent score (from Hans Zimmer and James Newton Howard) that is unrelenting but still mostly unobtrusive, a solid script and high production value lay the foundation from which the aforementioned excellent work is built. With the feel of a ridiculously polished (as it should be for $135 million) independent film, the Chicago-based Gotham City is edgier and darker than "Batman Forever", but grittier than Tim Burton's noir-ish films. Those were bleak by design, while Batman Begins seems to draw its bleakness from beyond mere physicality, from a hope-starved story that matches its dismal yet chimerical backdrop. Instead of the fact-based world of Spider-man and his New York City, Batman and his Gotham sport a fantasy-laced makeover that better allows for distinctions between good and evil. While moral murkiness fits some films ("Mystic River"), superhero flicks work best with clear-cut distinctions. By creating a city with a sense of elevated reality, director Christopher Nolan and company imbue "Batman Begins" with a stronger soul that thrives on the film's dominant theme of fear, compounding the movie's allure.All aspects collectively tap into the mysterious and powerful Batman myths better than any other movie in the franchise. We now know not just who and what Batman is, but how and why he exists.Bottom Line: "Batman Begins" is the best on-screen incarnation of the Dark Knight yet. A high 8 of 10.

Aside from a few ridiculous detours, this Batman is miles better than Batman Forever. It's also nowhere near Batman (or even Batman Returns) but most people won't care because it's also a lot funnier :) Here's where it all falls apart: a white guy (with a Korean name) flies into Tibet, taking over large portions of Asia's criminal underworld; with his new network of criminals, he builds a giant monastery to train the hordes of ninjas he will need to destroy Gotham City (which is halfway across the world). Sounds weak? It is, really, considering that none of it makes any sense from any angle the movie presents us with; however, spectacular execution and neat Bat-toys save this Batman from becoming another terrible Batman Forever-style turd. Christian Bale works hard to distract from the awful backstory he's given, and succeeds after the first hour is over. That hour, mind you, seems to last forever. Toke up and enjoy!

review: Great return of a non-childish hero
main_review: Making a superhero movie isn't easy, mainly because a lot of expectation is created something a lot of people has been reading in decades. The last two Batman movies where very childish for not to say very disappointing, but now Christopher Nolan presents a Batman that really makes sense. The story shows the why's and when's of the origin of the character in a way that could be possible (in a Jurassic Park way). The villains are not crazy psychopaths, but respectable criminals with strong foundations. Batman isn't Superman, he's a normal person, and you can sense that in the movie. The turns of the movie and the effects are very good, the hallucination scenes are really scary and the support characters have very good dialogues. The jokes are good but not so often giving seriousness. I would recommend it to everyone, but it can be confusing for children though.

He does have the build and looks especially good in the tux which i saw would of benefited him more as taking on the new bond role. Although i did find Neesons character and his gang an odd bunch, your built up that there's this guild of freedom fighters who stand in the face of injustice and protect the weak yet this is shattered and their acts at the finale of the movie are truly baffling and i wasn't convinced at all what and why they were in Gotham of all places. Thanks to the confusion who really is behind the criminality inside Gotham, the characters of scarecrow, falcone & ducard seem just a solidified goo inside your head, There isn't any focused attention and thus no reward for when they are caught. I would also argue batman was the direct result of the majority of violence on screen. There's a lot of complaining about Gotham that its destroying itself and the criminality is so high, yet there was only 1 proper scene of criminality before the finally.As for the cinematic of seeing batman perched on a roof gargoyle, i was only thinking you would of used a lift then awkwardly climb out of a window. i think this problem flows through the second part of the film, as it progresses he seems to take on more supernatural powers of being able to fly anywhere he likes. The fighting sequences were terribly shot as well, the cameras so focused in on the action, you only see fists flying and arms twisting everywhere i couldn't understand who was hitting who, i was only slightly surprised batman was left standing last after that mish-mash of body parts.i feel bad for criticising batman so bad as i was on such a high going into the cinema but halfway through i was bored to tears. It seems the hype and ego of "making The batman movie" got the better of the script writers and as a result the plot and character development suffers badly. I'm sure movie goers of 12-18 will love this film as it felt like it was written by children.

there are few people out there who love batman more than me. that said, i was very upset with joel schumacker for ruining the franchise. even batman returns fell short of my expectations. and if i were being truly honest, i would point out that even the original batman wasn't true to the comic book, and therefore not an accurate representation of batman. batman begins is the installment we should have seen way back in 1989. this movie has it all. it shows the origin of batman, beyond a crime in a back alley. this is what fans needed to see. the movie could not be better. i've heard that the movie failed to gross anywhere near the spiderman 2 release, and i blame a lack of aggressive advertising, and of course, 2 crappy batman movies in the last decade. this is important: ignore everything you know about batman so far. this is a whole new dark night. impressive all the way around.

review: Brilliant movie directed by a brilliant director
main_review: In 1989 the first Batman movie arrived, a good movie, but not awesome. Since then the Batman-movies got worse. Batman Returns was nice, Batman Forever was boring and Batman & Robin was just terrible...And then you hear another Batman movie is coming. I first thought 'Oh no, not again', but when I heard Christopher Nolan would direct the movie I got curious. I went to the cinema and all I can say is.....I have never seen such a good action movie, NEVER! The movie is not just about action and action, but also contains atmosphere, a good story and very good acting work (well done, Christian Bale!). The story is actually about Bruce Wayne and his inner demons, not Batman. It is about how the parents of Bruce were killed, the training of Bruce, how Bruce got all of his Batman-stuff and why he chooses the suit of a bat. Well all by all, you'll just have to see this movie...it is without doubt the best movie of 2005, and it will probably become a classic.

I didn't think I was going to live long enough to see a good Batman movie. I had given up all hope on this franchise, and they went and hired a director who could direct, actors who could act, and a writer who could write. Then, the kept the story and the gadgets and the action just plausible enough to create real excitement and suspense. Nolan demonstrated the obvious to the Hollywood crap-machine: stuff that is realistic is more engaging than stuff that feels fake.I have to call out the casting as being particularly good, especially given that Batman movies have become a career-ending cyanide tablet for the actors involved.

I truly have been a BatMan fan all of my life. I enjoyed the first two batman movies very much. Tim Burton did a great job on them. The last two seemed to go downhill rather quickly. It took a perfect cast and a perfect Director to resurrect the series, but here we are. Even though the film didn't quite stick with the other four Batman Movies, it still exceeded them. I was truly frightened by the villains and believed them. they aren't just people running around in colorful costumes trying to destroy Gothom for no reason at all. They were completely believable. Christian Bale did such a superb job as the title character. He really allowed us into the world of Batman and let me experience it through his eyes. Overall, one of the best i've seen in theaters this year.

review: Thank you Mr. Nolan & Mr. Bale for bringing the series back up to form where Mr. Burton & Mr. Keaton left off.
main_review: I'm a HUGE Batman fan!!! Batman in my book has always been the coolest comic book character. So needless to say the first two films "Batman" and "Batman Returns" which starred Michael Keaton and were directed by Tim Burton are two films I think of very highly in my book. But up next came the mediocre "Batman Forever" which is when both Mr. Keaton and Mr. Burton bailed and as their replacements we got Val Kilmer as the Dark Knight and Mr.Schmacher in the director's chair. Seeing this film made me lose a lot of interest in the character and franchise especially with Tommy Lee Jones as Two-Face and Jim Carrey as the Riddler. I do have to give Mr. Kilmer a little respect here, he was a decent Batman, and it wasn't his fault I didn't care too much for the film. It was the Robin character played by Chris O' Donnell, the villains, and a mediocre script that really turned me off about the film.But just after "Batman Forever," the biggest pile of crap to ever hit the Batman Franchise came along, and this of course was known as "Batman & Robin." "Batman & Robin" suffered from some of the worst casting (and acting) I ever seen in my life; Arnold Schwarzenegger as Mr. Freeze, George Clooney as Batman, and Alicia Silverstone as Batgirl just to name a few. Also throw in one of the worst scripts ever written with dialogue that a 5 year old could have written better ("Lets kick some Ice") and you have the huge pile of crap known as "Batman & Robin." So I thought my once favorite character Batman was dead in a deep, dark grave but long and behold 8 years after the disaster that was "Batman & Robin" comes "Batman Begins" a film with a solid cast and not to mention Batman played by Christian Bale and is directed by Christopher Nolan the man behind such great films like "Memento" and "Insomnia" I knew some good was still left in the series. How much? Well keep on reading to find out."Batman Begins" is just like its title suggests, it's the beginning and that's probably a good thing since I just explained what happened to the Batman franchise in the past. The movie starts off with the story behind Bruce Wayne (Christian Bale) and what happened to his family and so forth. It then moves into how he was trained and how he can fight the way he does. Then long and behold Bruce Wayne becomes Batman and wants to save the city of Gotham from the crime that has devoured the city.The final words in "Batman Begins" said something like this "I never got to say Thank you" and Batman turns around and says "You will never need to." I think I need to say thank you to Mr. Nolan and everyone involved. Thank you for bringing the Batman franchise back to its peak form. I would actually dare to say and this is coming from one of Tim Burton's biggest fans that Mr. Nolan has made a film on the same level as the original Batman. I never thought it could be done but it has and Mr. Nolan deserves most of the thanks not to mention the always fantastic Christian Bale as the Dark Knight, Gary Oldman as Commissioner Gordon, Michael Caine as Alfred, as well as Morgan Freeman as Fox, Liam Neeson as Ducard and Cillian Murphy as the scarecrow. The right casting definitely made a difference not to mention a great script and wonderful direction.The movie is a visual fest for the eyes with so much going on, it's almost a film you walk out of and want to run right back into to see it again. The special effects are wonderful and the whole background story with the Bats and the Batcave are interesting as well. Not to mention the new Batmobile which is just bad@ss and Bale's awesome yet cocky line when Freeman first shows him the car, "Does it come in black" is just awesome. Not to mention how perfectly timed everything was, the movie never seemed to drag, everything just fit into place even with a runtime of 2 hours and 20 minutes.The thing that worried me about "Batman Begins" was this, the last time a great independent film director made a mainstream movie we got "The Hulk" which was directed by Ang Lee the man behind "Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon" and "The Ice Storm." Needless to say "The Hulk" wasn't a very good movie in fact it pretty much sucked but Nolan on the other hand showed the world that a great independent director can also make a great mainstream big budget film and Nolan did this almost flawlessly.So in conclusion, if you're a Batman fan, you're in luck because Batman is back and is here to kick some serious ass. Batman is back in his top form with a new lead by Mr. Bale. The script is wonderful, the acting is terrific for a mainstream big budget flick, and the direction along with the cinematography is just stunning. I have been waiting 13 years to see a Batman film like this and I am glad that day has finally arrived. I hear a sequel is already in talks and they are talking about bringing back the Joker. As long as Nolan and Bale are still aboard for the sequel I am there opening day! Also I have some suggestions for Joker, I was thinking about it when the film ended and I think Johnny Depp or even Crispin Glover would be perfect for the role."Batman Begins" may actually be one of the best films of the year or at least of the summer. MovieManMenzel's final rating for "Batman Begins" is a 9/10. BATMAN RULES!!!

By far the best Batman since the first one and it definitely rivals, if not surpasses it, as the best of the bunch. The fact Christopher Nolan makes Gotham look real and gritty instead out of a comic book makes most of the movie work. Bruce Wayne's mystery is exposed from the beginning and Christian Bale does a great job as the title role. Michael Caine as witty Alfred was good. Gary Oldman was extremely believable as Gordon and pulled it off nicely. Lucius Fox was my favorite character--Morgan Freeman had fun with his role---he knew something was up and he knew it was for good. Katie Holmes was serviceable---she wasn't horrible as everyone says BUT she was miscast. They could have found someone else to played Dawes--she still comes of as the Dawson's Creek girl, and now, the Cruise spouse. Cilian Murphy will continue to get noticed as a versatile actor and he did good as Scarecrow. Overall--great film, mostly fine acting and a Batman that's gritty and realistic...a refreshing change from the overdone comic book excess that led to the series' initial demise in 1997.

I've always been a fan of the Batman series. Tim Burton created films with dark undertones and flamboyant villains. After he and Keaton left, the series became extremely epic if losing some of its appeal. I was beginning to think the series would never recover.Even in the Burton days, however, I always felt that something was missing from the series. The movies were great looking with great action, but they seemed to have a huge difficulty understanding why and how a rich orphan would be compelled to vigilante justice and dress like a flying mammal. When asked why in 1989's Batman, Wayne stated "Because no one else can." I liked the movie, but that just sounds like a bored writer taking the easy way out.Christopher Nolan, in this latest and greatest installment, has made an entire film on the premise of that question. He provides a deeper look into Bruce Wayne, who in the previous films was shown as a bored billionaire who wants to make some halfassed contribution to society by buying gadgets and hanging junkies off rooftops. Now, he's a tortured soul who comes to the realization that before he can exorcise Gotham's demons he has to exorcise his own.The film opens in a Tibetan prison where Wayne has confined himself so he can fight the inmates. When a hulking Asian goon informs him, "This is Hell and I am the devil," Bruce nonchalantly replies, "You're not the devil. You're practice," before unleashing his rage onto him and five other inmates. The guards lock him up for protection, but Bruce insists he needs none. "Not yours, theirs!" He is recruited by the League of Shadows and journeys into his own fears that he might turn it against the villains of Gotham. During this time, he is trained by Liam Neeson, who reveals harsh truths about his society, justice, and his past, "Your parents' death wasn't your fault...it was your father's!" Nolan delivers these philosophies as devoutly as DeMill delivered the Ten Commandments, but when Wayne's training ends, he realizes that the League is no less corrupt than the villains they fight.He returns to Gotham having destroyed the League's headquarters, killed all its members, and been declared legally dead after an eight year absence. He returns to a city that is not only corrupt and run down, but in denial. One of the things I loved about the film was the fact that it took time to develop Gotham's history. It never fully recovered from the Depression that hit it twenty years earlier, the city's worst criminals are running the show, and a deranged psychiatrist conducts unnatural experiments at Arkham Asylum.Bruce struggles to gain the necessary components to make Batman a reality while still maintaining a playboy persona to avoid suspicion. He slowly masses his resources while immediately plunging into war against an entire city of enemies. By the end of the film little has actually gotten better, but Gotham has a symbolic hope from their new hero. Bruce Wayne, however, has disappeared. He is a mask that Batman wears.This film is not afraid to delve into the true nature of the basest of human emotions and conditions. It provides honesty and realism to a genre that so often lacks it. The questions are not easy, but the answers are even harder.FOUR STARS...the best superhero film of all time

As a kid, I enjoyed comic books. Whenever I had the money, I would go to the corner store and pick up my favorites. But, unlike many comic book readers, I never really connected with Superman or Spiderman. For me it was always "Batman". Something about the gritty realism and dark atmosphere drew me in. I also respected the fact that Bruce Wayne never had to rely on superhuman abilities to get the job done.Needless to say, my expectations were quite high for this latest installment. And I was not disappointed in the least. As much as I adored the two film incarnations brought to the screen by Tim Burton (yes, I truly and completely enjoyed "Batman Returns"), I always felt something was lacking. The films, including the horrendous Joel Schumacher train wrecks, seemed to focus way too much on the villains (Jack Nicholson's Joker remains one of my all time favorite movie bad guys) and not enough on the protagonist, Bruce Wayne.This new "Batman" fixes this problem with a truly remarkable look at a tortured soul who decides not to turn his back on the city that took his parent's lives.Christian Bale was made to wear the Batsuit. He looks truly menacing and delivers his lines with growling intensity. The supporting cast is, for the most part, equally up to par. The only exception I have to this is Katie Holmes. She just doesn't seem all that believable in the role she is required to play. She's not really bad, just not that great. Michael Caine, Rutger Hauer, Morgan Freeman, Liam Neeson, and (in a surprising "good guy" role) Gary Oldman add some class to the proceedings.In regards to the action scenes, a very sensitive part of comic book adaptations, the film was truly remarkable. Part of Batman's strategy of fighting crime is to strike fear into the hearts of criminals, and this is where director Christopher Nolan really hits the mark. The first real scene of Batman taking on some thugs is filmed in such a way that it is difficult to truly see what is going on. This may sound sloppy or cheap, but it actually gives the feel of being attacked by some unknown creature, and the glimpses of the cape only adds to the thugs' terror.The movie features all the gadgets and gizmos you would expect from a Batman movie as well as a re imagined Batmobile that is quite an impressive vehicle. The dialog is great, as well as the appropriate moments of humor. As difficult as it is for me to admit this, this is the way Batman was meant to be (Sorry, Tim). A dark and gritty masterpiece.

You know, keep you interested, guessing, and lots of twists and turns and comic proverbs(quotes)that chil your spine. Batman started off in an excellent way because it kept you interested and wondering, however, the late part of the show to the end it dragged for me. I think the director of spider man has the best approach to these comic movies because to me he provides the intense,guessing, interesting stuff that comics give. OK, just my opinion but here you have it.

review: Batman begins; when reality inspires fiction
main_review: When I went to watch "Batman begins" I was skeptical about the possibility of content deeper than what ordinary computer effects, unrealistic fights and futuristic weapons could offer. Instead I was Sruck by a lot of the details that were inspired by the tragic terrorist events in the Unites States. Without any explicit reference,the art director,Christopher Nolan, has developed a series of topics that bring us from unrealistic human flights in a bat costume and improbable car chases back to recent events: don't the training camps on the top of the mountains in a frozen lake recall those of Al Qaeda in Afganistan? And the ethnicity of the local population that "hosts" the camp is distinctively different from the inhabitants of Gotham? What about the train going into the main city skyscraper, the Wayne building, with the sounds of the people screaming in the background: isn't it reminiscent of an airplane flying into the Twin Towers while people are screaming and running away? Note that the Wayne building is the center of economic power much like the Twin Towers; it is not a hospital as pointed out by Wayne senior himself; not a building to help sick people, the weak and nowadays neglected side of society. Instead, it is the place where rich people are looking for better ways to become even richer. What about the "terror motive"? All throughout the movie ordinary people are terrorized by something that actually doesn't exist in reality but only in their own imagination: is our society like this now? This doesn't mean that the terror crusaders don't exist; they do, and after training, they come back from abroad to brutally destroy the entire society by using its latest technological innovations in order to impose their own idea of justice, their own order, their own morality. They have been trained to apply these ideas by decapitating people, as the Talebans and Al Zarkawi do.But the movie makes a step forward past reality and offers a solution; only by imposing civil justice, and not by taking revenge as initially suggested by the killing of a killer (c.f. death penalty), can peace be recovered, order restored and the weak (e.g. like the kid near the end of the movie ) defended. The art director suggests how to cure this society and find its way out of terror. Before defeating the crusaders, we have to cure the cancer within our society (c.f. Falcone and the police corruption) because this is how terror has found its way in and even propagated to our water supply. We have to heal these "internal diseases" such as the savage economic power which splits the society into two groups: the extremely rich people (like the Wayne family) and the very poor ones (like the homeless and beggars in the parking lots), where the former live, "literally" and economically, on top of the latter and no middle class people exist in society.Only by dealing with these problems can we recover light & love which shine through in the last scene of the movie. Both disappeared after the killing of the Waynes giving rise to darkness, rain, hate and revenge. We can do this without rejection of or discontinuity with the past (the house will be built brick by brick as it was before). Before that, we have to find the courage to move on and destroy what is bad as Batman did.Finally we can fairly say that this movie is more about reality than about fiction. It makes us think how these two are entangled even tighter because of unprecedented technological developments.

review: A different kind of superhero movie. Go. See it.
main_review: Not for children.Not a "comic book movie." A number of critics decried the lack of biff-pow, obviously totally missing the point. While this uniquely American legend was engendered by a comic, it can stand alone, as well.The Gotham of Burton was fantasy: the architecture in particular. The Gotham of Schumacher was loud, garish, over the top, both overtly and suggestively.This Gotham is a more realistic landscape filled with characters that can be believed as well as those that must be imagined.I didn't think I'd like Bale, but in one scene in particular, his anger was so palpable as to be genuinely intimidating. Wow.While Katie Holmes' character did have its place, I was left without much impression of her.Gary Oldman proved once again that he is a chameleon. Just a great job, ditto Freeman and Neeson. I couldn't imagine an Alfred other than Michael Gough, yet Michael Caine was a pleasant surprise.What startled me among the cast, however, was the first appearance of Cillian Murphy. I had never seen him and was astonished at his appearance, which was Tom Welling with a Dean Cain overlay. Looking at photos later, I found pictures of Murphy and Welling that could have been the same person, and couldn't help but wonder if Murphy had ever been considered for Superman.Whatever tack is taken on the Joker, next time, it will be quite different than Nicholson's, of necessity-- most likely, playing up the deeply evil nature of the crazy beast without much of the humor that made Jack palatable. The Joker's humor was horrible, sick, anything but funny. It will take a masterful rendition to match the rest of the characterizations thus far.And, finally, thank God there was a real music score! No transitory pop, no hip-hop, no blare in your ear garbage that panders to kids, but a real, orchestral treatment of emotion that enhanced--effectively, understatedly--everything else that was going on. If only other movies would recognize the value of treating music as of creative importance to a film.Altogether, a fine, fine effort. Now that the stage is set, the next installment should point up refinement and execution of the Batman's strategies...as well as his thinking on the fly...

review: A Fresh Breath to the Franchise
main_review: Christopher Nolan has never disappointed me. He has a strong sensibility for film noir detective stories as evidenced by Following, Memento, and Insomnia. Each of these films follows a troubled protagonist who must overcome personal adversity to accomplish a goal-- in most cases, revenge. Nolan, it seems, was the most logical choice of current directors to tackle the new Batman franchise.From the get-go we are thrust into Nolan's world of quick edits, skewed time frames, and clever back-stories. We absorb a large amount of information about Bruce Wayne's life in a relatively short time spanwho he is, what he wants, and most importantly, how much butt he can kick. The first half of the film plays like a traditional Nolan film with strong character development and solid storytelling. As if that weren't good enough, it soon takes a turn for the betterBatman quite literally begins.The great thing about this film is its possibility for widespread appreciation. Comic book aficionados will no doubt welcome the careful attention to Batman's history (as told through the original graphic novels, not other Batman movies, cartoons, or TV shows). But being an uber-geek isn't necessary to enjoy the movie. If you suspend your disbelief enough, you can almost fathom a scenario in which a rich man like Bruce Wayne could make this transformation. Like in the first Spiderman movie, we come to see depth of character rather than just a guy in tights and a mask.This is by far the grittiest of the Batman films, if not the darkest. Where Tim Burton did a good job of creating a Gotham City full of exaggerated shadows on a sound stage, Nolan uses real streets of Chicago and camera tricks to create the Dark Knight's home. The two styles are different, but this one ultimately feels more real. I recommend Batman Begins to theatergoers who are willing to follow moderately complicated plot lines in addition to great fight sequences and car chases.

main_review: The brain is like a video tape recorder... it will remember whatever you put on tape, easily erased and replaced by another image. Perfect casting, despite the mousy, teenagerish Holmes cast as a tough talking District Attorney (gladly no forced performances of her in action in the court room.. maybe one scene i cant remember). I especially enjoyed the casting of Cillian Murphy as the Scarecrow. A preppy neat metro-sexual type, nerdish but slightly off, as if you cant put your finger on it but there's something wrong with that Crane guy. It's always the quiet ones.... The hallucinogenic scenes are done quite well without needing much over-the-top CGI. A deliciously dark tone to the movie, needed like a shot in the arm.I think what everyone agrees with here is that this is not if not the second best, THE best Batman movie (next to the 1960s movie! :-) I'm sorry i love the schtick of the Adam West era Batman). Even more so, you can actually envision this being almost believable, as this dark and dingy world we're thrown in is somewhere we've either been or can be in if we don't keep our cities safe.Bravo.... A classic hero movie.

There really are no weak actors in the film, despite other peoples claims on Katie Holmes being the weak link, she did not due a bad job, she just looks to young for the part.WB decided to start over in the franchise, and let Christopher Nolen, director of such films as Momento and Insomnia give his take on the way Batman should be. review: A Very Good Batman.  In fact, the best Batman yet.
main_review: No movie is perfect, but this is certainly one heck of a good Batman. What is especially impressive is the intergenerational viewpoint of the director. I normally do not seek out, or even notice, references to other films when going to a movie, but I thought I detected visual references to Clockwork Orange in some of the scenes with Liam Neeson. Perhaps I'm just imagining it, though Christopher Nolan's biography on IMDb.COM indicates that he's a big fan of Stanley Kubrick, the director of Clockwork Orange.I was impressed by the subtle and somewhat more intellectual underpinnings of the film than what one might expect from a summer blockbuster. To bring a political quotation into this review, it's as if Nolan had taken to heart FDR's famous dictum that there is "nothing to fear but fear itself." If anything, the fight against fear is at least as important in the film as the fight against evil. That, in fact, seems to be the source from which Batman draws his strength in his fight against evil. The evil in the film is not just of the black and white variety either, but occupies a much grayer area. Official corruption, poverty, and the misuse of psychiatry (a la the Soviet Union's Serbsky Clinic, perhaps) are elements seamlessly blended in with the obvious evil of old-fashioned Gotham gangsterism. This is quite a heady diet for a summer blockbuster film, I'd say.Christian Bale is a fine Batman, and his supporting actors are as good as one could hope for, especially the wonderful Michael Caine as Alfred the Butler and Liam Neeson as Batman's mentor. Tom Wilkinson, too, is very believable as a Gotham godfather, and Rutger Hauer seems to be a perfect fit for the director of Wayne family business.This movie seems, therefore, to have it all: a good story, fine actors, and, if you are of a mind to entertain them, some deeper questions about what really constitutes good and evil.The darkness and themes of the movie may be too strong for children younger than 11-12 years old, I think, but for everyone else looking for a good summer movie I'd very much recommend it.

To be honest, I wasn't really looking forward to this movie - the promos looked dull and the memory of "Batman and Robin" still lingers... but what a pleasant surprise! This is not a traditional "superhero" movie. Rather, it plays like a character-driven thriller/adventure that just happens to be about a superhero.I was surprised at how real and logical (within the context of the movie) they kept everything. There was a rawness to this movie that worked really well. And I'm completely on board with the two decisions that have drawn some criticism - the new Batmobile, and the raspy "Batman voice". This is not the cool, wisecracking, understated Batman of yore - this is a hurt, angry, driven guy whose motivation is crystal clear by the time he dons the batsuit. And for the first time, we have an ambiguous, frightening Batman. I can see why criminals would run from this creature.A word about the cast - Christian Bale is an inspired choice, Michael Caine brings a much-needed dose of warmth and humor to the enterprise, and Morgan Freeman classes up pretty much anything he's in. Katie Holmes was miscast - would have preferred to see one of the L&O girls (Stephanie March?) in the role. Can't wait to see who they pick as the Joker for the sequel.

review: Now we know where he gets all those wonderful toys....
The greatest superhero film ever made.
main_review: I'd been excited for this movie before I ever saw a single trailer; Before I knew anything about the story, and before I knew of any of the cast save one member: Christian Bale, who along with Ewan Macgregor, happens to be my favourite actor. As a child, Batman was always my favourite super hero. He always seemed, to me, so Human. Much more believable than a teenager being bitten by a radioactive spider (Don't get me wrong, I love Spidey, he's my favourite next to The Caped Crusader). I was rather obsessive when I was young, and must have had just about every action figure and vehicle for the Batman: The Animated Series line from Kenner. I also have two favourite Supervillains: Venom, and of course, The Scarecrow. Something about a villain who destroys people by exposing them to their deepest fears to the point of insanity or mental breakdown just appeals to me. It seems the most sinister form of evil. Going into the movie, I admit, I already had (possibly unfairly) high expectations; something about my favourite actor portraying my favourite superhero just simply appealed to me, I suppose. All throughout, and at the end, I realized that the film far surpassed even my highest expectations. Bale perfectly captured the darkness, the barely-checked fury that I've always viewed as a defining element of The Dark Knight. The many small subtleties did wonders, as well, such as Bale subtly altering the tone and depth of his voice when he was behind the cowl. The action scenes were frenetic and beautifully choreographed. The small dash of humour contained in the movie was simply perfect, coming at just the right moments. One of my only qualms with the movie was Michael Caine's portrayal of Alfred. Not knocking his excellent (as always) performance, his acting was superb, and his wit very welcome. He just did not fit my ideal of Alfred, but that's entirely a matter of personal preferences. I found the acting to be superb in itself, which is all too uncommon in superhero movies. Bale, of course, was perfect as the dark, brooding, angry Bruce Wayne, and his alter ego. Cillian Murphy was perfectly unsettling in his portrayal of the outwardly calm, cool, intelligent Dr. Jonathan Crane, and even better as the creepy, psychotic scarecrow. Which brings me to my second qualm. My memory of The Scarecrow (which may not be precisely correct) was of a slightly more deranged, slightly more homicidal person. Perhaps in the future, if he recurs in the next films, he may be so. But I kept expecting to see him wearing the full straw-man ensemble, not just the burlap mask, and was a bit disappointed when it never happened. It didn't really detract from the experience, however, as Cillian's performance kept me more than appeased. Liam Neeson's performance was awe-inspiring, as always, though I can't say too much about it without giving the story away. Even the usually cringe-worthy Holmes wasn't completely unbearable or childish. The CG was tastefully done and not overused, thus making the movie a prime example of how CG effects can enhance a movie and make it more enjoyable. Gotham City was as dark and distopian as I've ever imagined it to be, and the Kowloon-inspired slums were a perfect touch. Here's to hoping Nolan and Bale stick together and make a few sequels, and even more so, here's to hoping they maintain a consistent level of perfection. 10/10.

I've been waiting for this since first seeing the cast listing, and have not been disappointed. Christian Bale makes a great lead, as he has done in so many things before, and deserves the A-List status this will give him. Subtle differences in voice and mannerisms between the 3 characters he plays (Bruce, Batman, and "Playboy Billionaire" Bruce) work really well, thought his raspy voice as Batman is a bit comical at times. It does mean however that you get an insight into what he's thinking, and how he breaks character when talking to certain people.The rest of the cast are as solid as you would expect of their calibre. Michael Caine gives some good comic relief as Alfred. Gary Oldman makes a decent Jim Gordon, and while he isn't given too much to do, you can imagine the character growing more over time and sequels. Morgan Freeman is, again unfortunately, not given too much to do, but gets his point across.Cillian Murphy is a bit of a surprise package as Crane, and I say Crane specifically, and not Scarecrow. Scarecrow does little more than hide behind some impressive special effects. Crane however exudes a creepy aura that makes you think of a smart geeky kid who was bullied in school, but snapped and went quietly psycho.The main flaw however is that while Chris Nolan is a great director for mood and angst, his action leaves a lot to be desired. The first time Batman emerges, it's a great little sequence of machine-gun wielding baddies running around a maze of cargo containers, while being menaced by a mysterious black shape, as their number are slowly swooped on and pulled away. It reminded me of "Predator" or "Alien" more than anything else. But whenever a real hand-to-hand fight occurs it seems to change to an overly-shaky camera style, with capes and scenery getting in the way of anything. This includes the ending of the cargo scene, where Batman drops into the centre of a group of six or seven baddies. The last time Christian Bale was surrounded by baddies in a fight was a few times in the underrated "Equilibrium", and those fights had humour and imagination in bucket loads. I appreciate the difference in psychology between fights in the training monastery, and the mysterious Batman stalking the streets, but all to often nothing the fights devolve into little more than chaotic sprawling of limbs for a few seconds at a time. Since Wayne is now a supposedly super-trained martial arts expert, with loads of new toys, you would hope that some innovation and novelty could have been built into this. Bring Kurt Wimmer in on the next one as adviser, and I'll be happy.Oh, and the Bat-Mobile is cool. The line about "Does it come in black?" was great. The next 37 jokes about it being cool started to drag...Bring on the next one, though what they call that is beyond me. "Batman continues"?

review: A super-hero movie about a real hero
main_review: Fans of the series rejoice in the truly awesome "Batman Begins".Director Chris Nolan brings us an exciting and intense Batman movie that most of us have been waiting for since Batman Returns, and it is has revolutionized the series beyond leaps and bounds.I will begin with that casting, Christian Bale is in my mind the new Batman without hesitation. He brings back the dark knight feel that Kilmer and Clooney lost. He also brings a genuine fear to the character that allows us to realize why the city might be afraid of its own shadow.Michael Caine is an Alfred who is finally a character with some emotion and a real intensity behind all his lines, he no longer feels like a stock character. Master actor Liam Neeson commands the screen when ever he is on it, and does the film an unlimited number of wonders. It's difficult to imagine anyone else in his role. And finally, Cillian Murphy plays the perfect villain with an almost innocent sense of evil that is very difficult to put into words. There are also strong performances from Morgan Freeman, Gary Oldman, and Tom Wilkinson.I was on the edge of my seat through out nearly the entire film, I was always wondering what was going to happen next or where Batman was going to pop out from, and when he did decide to the adrenalin rush that followed was worth seeing the movie for in itself.My favorite aspect of this film was its feel of realism, it wasn't over done of fantasized in nearly any way, and we feel that we are watching a man who is doing what we feels he must, and that what we are watching may all possibly be happening in some dark city right now. We are able to see eye to eye with the caped crusader in many ways because we have all experienced loss, and have often done nothing about it. But it is the fact that Batman takes the law into his own hands for justice that makes him the hero we love to watch.The only thing I could complain about in this film is that there was perhaps not quite enough of Batman on the screen, and maybe a little too much Bruce Wayen. However this is justified by the fact that it is a prequel and it isn't until somewhere in the half point that the Black Knight makes his triumphant appearance.All and all it is nice to see a film that wasn't afraid to say "all right, this is the way everything happened and you're going to like it", but this this film does, and it might have been considered a gamble, but it pays off in the end, because we now have fresh start to the Batman legacy.

review: "It's not who I am underneath, but what I do that defines me."
main_review: Very, very good movie. Easily the best comic book movie ever, and that's saying a lot because I loved Hellboy, The Punisher and the X-men and Spider-man films.The cinematography is brilliant. We're finally seeing Batman in 2.40:1, folks, and it shows. Every shot is composed wonderfully, and the darkness is almost like a character in itself.It's so much better than the first four Batman films that they can't even compare. Every member of the cast shines, particularly Bale. He's definitely the most convincing Batman we've yet seen.They need to make, like, six more of these movies.This is just a masterpiece. Everyone do yourselves a favor and go see it as many times as you possibly can.

The last two Batman films were the very definition of "summer blockbusters" and "popcorn" flicks. If you liked those, run along home because Batman Begins is above you.Comic to film conversions have enjoyed a renaissance since Spiderman and films like this make me glad this is so. It proves that you don't need to obliterate the continuity of the comic to make the transition from paper to celluloid. This film accurately captures the essence of the comics in a way that not even Spiderman achieved.This is by no means a standard action film. If anything, to call it an action film is a misnomer. The action isn't thin on the ground but it's not exactly abundant either. This fits in perfectly with the feel of the film though. It's as much about the characters as it is about things exploding and therein lies the strength of the film.Even the weakest link - Katie Holmes - manages to give a reasonable performance and most of the others (Bale and Caine especially) do justice to their roles. Not only that but the plot is not driven by the action but vice-versa, hence the more sensible amounts. Though the actual combat scenes tend to favour the "too fast and close to see anything" style of cinematography that has been on the rise since the mid 90s.In any event, despite these problems, the film itself will draw in fans and casual viewers alike but if you're looking for a load of explosions, a lack of plot and dialogue exclusively in one-liners... well, just stay at home.

review: This Ain't No Kids Comic Book
main_review: The other feature films called "Batman" are to this movie what a Saturday morning ABC Family show is to "The Godfather." A very powerful, superbly directed movie with a treasure trove of name actors that make it all the more enjoyable. And the new kids in the movie -- Christian and Katie -- deliver solid performances that are definitely not the bubble gum pap we've been served up in the other "Batmans." (If only these two could have starred in Star Wars rather than the boring, wooden Hayden and Natalie!) It's a bit on the long side, but I can't honestly say there were more than a few minutes that should've been left on the cutting room floor.If your senses can take it, sit close to the screen in a new theater with a really good sound system. It will rattle you in more ways than one.

review: A satisfying reinvention of the dying movie franchise.
Chris Nolan, Chris Nolan, (out)does everything Sam Raimi can
main_review: Batman has always been my favorite comic book hero. I remember watching Batman tens of times, being scared a lot by the Penguin in Batman Returns ( I was 10 years old when it came out ), loving the action sequences of Batman Forever, and then Batman & Robin was released, and as you already know it was of the worst movies ever made. After Batman & Robin, I lost any hope of seeing another Batman movie.So I was surprised to know that they were making another Batman movie. I was equally surprised by the talents attached to the movie in front of and behind the camera. I thought "this movie might be half as good as the Spiderman movies". The Spiderman movies were in my opinion the best comic movies ever made, and that totally changed when I saw Batman Begins.First things first, Batman Begins is not a sequel nor a prequel to the old Batman movies. It assumes the old movies never happened. It re-tells the story of Bruce Wayne in a whole different way. It begins by Bruce Wayne as a kid, how his fear of bats began, how his parents died, the reasons of his anger, etc.This movie is quite the opposite of the old movies. One of the main problems of the original series is that too much attention and screen time were given to the villains, Robin & Batgirl, and as a result Batman was almost a secondary character. That's not the case here. The character of Bruce Wayne is the main focus here, I can even say that Scarecrow needed to be shown a little bit more.Batman Begins is very dark, which brings it closer to the spirit of the comic books. This movie is definitely not for children. Some of the scenes with Scarecrow are scarier that any horror movie released this year.Christian Bale was excellent as Bruce Wayne / Batman. I liked the way he changed his voice when he was Batman to scare his enemies more. The supporting cast ( with the exception of Katie Holmes, which wasn't given much to do anyway ), were as good as Bale, especially Morgan Freeman & Micheal Caine.I definitely think Chris Nolan is the reason why the movie is so good. Instead of making Batman Begins a dumb action movie, he created a character movie, with some action scenes here and there. I've read that some people didn't like the one-to-one fights because the camera was so close and shaky. I think this was Nolan's intention, as we see the fights from the point of view of the criminals. I think the first fight, where we don't see Batman at all, but instead we see the criminals thrown to the left and to the right is an instant classic.So why do I think this movie is better than the Spiderman movies? Well, as I said, because it is darker, the movie is closer to the spirit of the comics than any Spiderman movie . Box office wasn't in the mind of Chris Nolan when he made this movie. He didn't make a movie for the box office, he made the movie he wanted. There are no romantic scenes to attract the ladies, the movie is too scary for the kids, and the whole first hour is Batman-less. And as the early box office figures show, the movie is making only a fraction of the money Spiderman ( or Spiderman 2 ) made. I'm sure 10 years from now, everybody will say how Batman Begins is the best comic movie made.So, I highly recommend watching Batman Begins, and let's just all hope that this movie will be decent hit so that we could see a sequel.

Let me start by saying that I am not a comic-book (or graphic novel) fan, and so my knowledge of the Batman oeuvre is limited. I don't know if the comics address the subject matter of this movie, and I refuse to debate whether the Batman backstory developed in this film is true to the original.That said, what most impressed me about the film was its very clean, believable storyline. From previews and magazine articles, I feared that the backstory would simply be Zen-this, Matrix-that. But the motivation behind the training sequences was very consistent with Bruce Wayne's known psyche, and the mutual attraction between the League of Shadows and Bruce Wayne was believable. In addition, Bruce Wayne's descent from tragically orphaned little boy to super-man followed a very sensible, linear path (if your sensibility is as skewed as Bruce Wayne's). Throughout the film, Bruce's and Batman's motivations and decisions consistently looped back to the mentality formed in Bruce Wayne's childhood, creating a compelling, focused character that was born in childhood and developed through experiences we were able to see on film.I would be remiss if I left out the casting and performance of Christian Bale. What a truly inspired choice! He comes into the film with a reputation and history of playing anti-social characters, and that reputation enhances our belief in Bruce Wayne's sociopathy. He is never properly adjusted to his surroundings: as young Bruce, he abandoned the mores of the society he was born into; as a trainee, he does not proceed in lockstep with his savior; as Bruce Wayne, he exhibits a certain disaffect if not disdain for his station in life; and as Batman, he is more evil than good.Christopher Nolan's Gotham remains dark without the surreal aspects of Tim Burton's or the goofiness of Joel Schumacher's.I consider this easily the best Batman movie I've seen and I am looking forward to the next installment.

when i found out they were making another batman movie last year, i have to say this was unpleasant news at the time. not since batman returns have i enjoyed seeing a batman movie in the theatre. i hate to knock on batman forever and batman and robin...........no i don't! i will say this, its obvious to say that the sequels created after Tim Burton left the project did not live up to our expectations. in all honesty, after Michael Keaton left the project, i think we were all done. no one has been able to carry the cape like Keaton did. up until last night did i believe that. An excellent, well-conceived, well-acted and exciting movie. I loved Batman Begins! Christian Bale is the best Batman to date in my opinion. No one has ever done the "Batman voice" as well as he. The one thing I would perhaps consider missing is a powerful Batman music score.I just remember how moving Danny Elfman's Batman theme was in the original 1989 Batman. But, I can live without that. Everything else more than makes up for that small detail. This movie works on so many different levels. I can't stop thinking about it! I am eagerly anticipating the sequel. 10 STARS!

This Batman movie was definitely not like the others. a) because it had none of the cast from the others and b) because it was filmed in a different style and of course c) it was darker.But that doesn't mean it was bad. I thought it was great.It goes into a lot of detail on how Bruce Wayne became Batman. And not just a wee intro thing, it was a large part of the movie.At the beginning it cuts back and forth between present and past, which may make you confused ( I understood it all, but I was with friends who weren't following it) but it stays in present for the rest.I thought the story was very smart. It had Batman villains (with funny beards!) that we don't normally hear about which was interesting.The comic relief was good. Some laugh out loud moments and some things you'll probably find funny that aren't meant to be.There are some really good action scenes. Very exciting and original.Acting was good. What can I say that hasn't already been said. I love this movie! The acting is great. The story is great. The visual style is a mix of noir and gritty surrealism. The villains(Cillian Murphy in particular)are finally menacing and not a bunch of goofy looking morons making lame jokes, as in the previous two "Batman" films. I also must agree with many others that Christian Bale may well be the best Batman ever. This movie also had a surprising amount of humor, so as not to drown itself in complete seriousness as some critics were suggesting it did. I loved everything about this film, but my favorite part is the little surprise Nolan has waiting for fans at the end. If you haven't seen this movie yet, I suggest you drop everything and do so. If you have, then see it again, as I intend to do! 10/10

I expected this movie to be enjoyable when I sat down to watch it. I was enticed by the trailers and was ready to be impressed. The first ten minutes of the film had me rolling my eyes and questioning every directorial decision by Nolan. Where was this movie going! Suddenly, it clicked. Ducard showed up in Wayne's cell and from that point forward I was in heaven. First ten minutes of skepticism forgotten.Everything about this film I found fantastic. The performances, for example. Brilliant. Christian Bale shines as Bruce Wayne in a way Keaton never could have. Michael Caine provides some dry humor while being utterly believable as a caring confidant. Cillian Murphy's understated Crane was deliciously creepy and smug, and the Scarecrow scenes were inventive and fresh. Liam Neeson was goddamn extraordinary. Rutger Hauer/Morgan Freeman were decent, and Katie Holmes serviceable.I wish the other Batman films had never been made. This is not a prequel, folks: this is a re-start. Burton's films, while in line with his body of work (quirky, creative masterpieces), are NOT true Batman films. Keaton sleepwalks through the role and Batman is done a disservice. Bale nails both Wayne and Batman in a way never captured in a live-action film before.Found the scene where Bruce's parents are murdered surprisingly powerful. Nolan truly is a dramatic talent. THe entire Bruce Wayne backstory borders upon brilliant, with bale and neeson proving they are incredible actors who can deliver a believable yet forceful performance.Yes, the action is choppy, and yes, the film ends jaggedly. What happened in the aftermath of the fear toxin? Never explained. Very minor quibbles. These are the only faults I can find with this film.The score is perfect, the performances fantastic, the writing very decent (some corny one liners could have been excised, but who's counting). All in all, an incredibly film that I saw twice and loved both times. This movie needs to be enjoyed by everyone, so that a sequel can be made. Please see this movie. Nolan can learn from his mistakes and improve upon his triumphs. The next film can only get better. See it so there will be a next film! And forget the crappy Burton Batmans ever existed - these movies are different and better.10/10

Batman Lives. I've waited a long time for this day, this hour, this minute. Years before i used to contemplate various ways i could think of to bring back the dark knight's respect to the audience. From plot development to specific fight scenes to villain type because i was so tired of the low attention these scriptwriters, these directors gave to our favorite man in black. Finallly the Bat thats been haunting my childhood dreams and mutating my nightmares has become my reality and i couldn't be happier.The beginning sets up the entire Bruce Wayne past(childhood, Murder, ETC.) and usually this would seem a bore, but with the training it shows him go through, your not in such a rush to move on. In this movie, Batman is darker than ever, and i mean DARK. Way darker than in Batman by Tim Burton. Not to discredit his film, but he's dark and fans are gonna love this. The film does not seem rushed, the script is well written and well performed. This whole film is beautiful. review: The kind of Superhero movie America has been needing
main_review: The incredible success of superhero movies, such as X-men I and II and Spiderman I and II, has left a bad taste in my mouth. Not that X-men or Spiderman franchises are bad. I for one am very much looking forward to Spiderman III, the problem is, that both movies are much too Americanized. And the following formula used for the movies is why: 1. Focus on heros that suffer ridicule because they have supernatural powers. 2. Make sure to get a couple camera shot of shapely woman, but remember to keep a PG-13 rating. 3. More scary the villain, the sweeter the success of the hero(s). 4. Keep the plot SIMPLE.Batman, however, is not some cookie cutter summer blockbuster movie (although I do hope it does well at the box office). And this is why it is different, and better then all the other recent comic book to big screen adaptations: 1. Batman doesn't have any superpowers, so he's much more relate-able 2. No slutty shots of girls to cheapen the movie. 3. More complex and purposeful the villain, the sweeter the success. 4. Plot is complex enough, so as to not be overly predictable.In a nutshell, I personally left the theater after seeing Spiderman 2, very entertained. After Batman Begins; a better man.

I'm 49. I've been around through all sorts of versions of Batman. I can recall the Silver Age Batman (which also included Batwoman, Bat-Girl and Bat-Mite and Ace the Bat-Hound..yes, BAT-HOUND). I watched as Batman came to the TV screen with Adam West. I've seen the Burton Batmans and the Shumacher Batmans...I've seen frank Miller's Batman etc etc..... This film was good. It had its strong points. It was certainly better than the last few films. CBale was great and the supporting cast was excellent. But I'm not sure why everyone is falling over themselves in praise for the film. Sure, it's entertaining and mostly never dragged. But it just didn't seem all that classic or GREAT.I cant say what was missing for me or what would have made it better (I'd give it a B+ or 3 stars) but I prefer BATMAN with Keaton and Nicholson myself. I enjoyed the film but can't say I'd ever sit through it again. It was dark and gritty and clever..... I enjoyed THE SHADOW (1994) more with its 1030's style and wit. I wouldn't say this revolutionized the comic book movie. It borrowed from what's already been done in the comics to revolutionize comics. I didn't see it as leaps and bounds better than the SPIDERMAN films or X-MEN films. Don't get me wrong...I liked it ..but not enough to say it's the best ever comic book film or even the best version of Batman ever done.

review: Everything about this movie was awe-inspiring
main_review: The action sequences, the backstory, the characters and most superb of all- the CAST- make this one of the best movies of 2005. The entire film was a delight for the senses, and I as I came out of the first showing, I got right back in line to buy a ticket for another showing next week.Christian Bale is in superb form here, striking the perfect note as the confident, young, Bruce Wayne, but also there are notes of vulnerability that he brings to the performance that make us truly believe how tortured he is inside. Liam Neeson was in excellent form as Wayne's teacher/nemesis and has proved yet again what an asset to the movies he is. Michael Cain and Morgan Freeman have graced us yet again with brilliant turns in characters that they were almost born to play.Cillian Murphy was the ultimate villain, with an appearance so striking that he stole every scene he was in. The only weak spot was Katie Holmes, but it was not enough to detract from the film. Gary Oldman brought such an intense believability to his character, showing us his good, humble roots, that we can forever say goodbye to the fat, cartoonish Comissioner Gordon from the previous films. The ending leaves open the possibility of a sequel as well, so there is much to look forward to.Finally- this movie is not suited to children. Though it gets a PG-13 rating for lack of strong language and nudity, there is a lot of violence and subject matter too difficult and scary for small children to tackle. I wouldn't recommend this movie to any child under the age of 10, or maybe even 12.

Batman has always been my favourite comic book character. "Batman Begins" is the long-awaited screen return of the Caped Crusader, whose last outing in "Batman & Robin" (1997) met with disastrous results. Here, the DC Comics titan of the title is given a fresh start by director Christopher Nolan ("Memento," "Insomnia") and a new (albeit) unlikely face to boot - Christian Bale. Nolan's (mostly) brilliant film is an exercise of sheer timing and is something that even the most devout of "Batman" purists can (finally) appreciate.Tim Burton's 1989 film adaptation of the "Batman" legend returned the character to the darker, grittier, more noirish origins Bob Kane had envisioned, and is perhaps the best screen vision of the Dark Knight. The Gotham City in that picture was a decaying metropolis that was overrun with crime and corruption, and though many decried the casting of Michael Keaton as Bruce Wayne, he nonetheless fit the bill perfectly by exuding the moodiness and torment of the character he was playing.Burton's film was something extraordinary in the making as well, being that it was influenced greatly by the works of Frank Miller, namely "The Dark Knight Returns" and "Year One," both of which apparently also played a hand into Nolan's picture. But since "Batman Begins" takes place before Burton's films (and Nolan's vision discards that arc entirely), any comparisons are void and a waste of time and therefore, it must be judged on its own merits.To me, Batman is the most mythical and mysterious of superheroes, being he's a playboy and a brilliant philanthropist but suffers from deep psychological issues and is missing a few screws from an otherwise well-oiled machine. That quality of mysticism, to me, is at the heart of this dark and mysterious character known as the Batman, who "would have to be some kind of a freak to go out at night dressed up as a bat."Nolan's film dives right into the character of Bruce Wayne and his metamorphosis into the Dark Knight of Gotham City. As the film opens, we see Wayne (played wonderfully by Bale) is being held prisoner by Henri Ducard (Liam Neeson) and his minions. Recognizing the anger festering inside him, Ducard appoints himself Wayne's mentor and begins training him for his (not yet realized) destiny.Years have passed since Bruce left Gotham City to travel the globe, never to return, after his parents were murdered and the man responsible was executed outside the courthouse. While here, he enters into harsh training with the League of Shadows, a band of stealth vigilante ninjas who have an apparent organization all over the world, not just in the mountains of Asia.But when Bruce draws a line between being judge and executioner, he becomes a marked man by the League, and makes mortal enemies out of Ducard and the group's leader Ra's Al Ghul (Ken Watanabe). Meanwhile in Gotham, things have gotten steadily worse since Bruce forced himself into exile away from the city. On the business front, Bruce must contend with a ruthless corporate raider (Rutger Hauer), and a powerful gangster named Carmine Falcone (Tom Wilkinson) controls the city's central criminal elements and assistant D.A. Rachel Dawes (Katie Holmes) - who's also a childhood friend of Bruce - is trying her best to find a way to have him incarcerated.Falcone's wave of terror, however, is mere child's play compared to the scheme being orchestrated by corrupt Arkham Asylum psychiatrist Dr. Jonathan Crane (Cillian Murphy), who moonlights as a hooded maniac called "the Scarecrow" and is unearthing plans to contaminate Gotham's water supply with a powerful hallucinogenic drug that when vaporized and inhaled, will drive the denizens of the crime-ridden Narrows insane and then they'll begin to tear the city apart. When it becomes apparent that Crane is not working alone in his devious plans and that he is merely a pawn being used by a mysterious third party, Bruce is forced to spring into action as Batman."Batman Begins," put simply, is a comic book fan's dream; I don't have any other way to describe it. Like last year's "Spider-Man 2," a lot more is done right than wrong. Nolan's film exhibits all of the best qualities of the Dark Knight by shying away from any camp elements and creating a vision that's not only bold and faithful to its source material (and most rabid of fans), but is also quite scary. I guess that I should also make it clear that this is by no means a children's movie, despite its now-kid-friendly "PG-13" rating.When Wayne first dawns the Batsuit, he's quite naturally clumsy, so it takes him a while to get used to it. And of course with the help of his faithful butler Alfred (Michael Caine), weapons designer Lucius Fox (Morgan Freeman) who first introduces us to the bad-ass Batmobile that would make Hummer and Cadillac both blush with envy, and the only honest cop left in Gotham City - James Gordon (Gary Oldman), Batman is able to restore some order to the city.Christian Bale is cast amazingly well, almost surely joining the ranks of Keaton, who without any bias is my preferred choice for the role of the Dark Knight. Bale is cool when he has to be playboy Bruce, but when it comes time for action in the Batsuit, he takes on a whole new dimension. This is the first film of Christopher Nolan's that I've truly liked, and his direction here is standout, making this Batman that much more brooding and haunted. He also effectively cast much of Gotham in impenetrable shadows, thus making it the most distinct place of any movie today and almost making it impossible to see what's in that alley some character is walking into."Batman Begins" is not your father's Batman, and that's a good thing. It's a triumph of timing and skill, and as the film's ending would have it, sequels are most definitely on the way.10/10

review: I hate to say this, but it's much more impressive than Tim Burton's
main_review: Although i'm a huge fan of Tim Burton's, i didn't like what he did to Batman. He put far too much humor in his Batman movies. It was funny sometimes, but I always had a feeling like: No, this is wrong, this isn't supposed to be a comedy movie. I thought it would be Burton-style, but i was COMPLETELY wrong. It even was a tearjerker movie! So yeah, i did cry when Bruce Wayne lost his parents. That scene and the ones that come after are so touching. And of course Christian Bale is a very attractive, charming Batman, he has a great warm voice and he's even better than Clooney. I never thought there would be a better and more handsome Batman than Clooney. This movie proves me wrong. The bad guy in this movie (i can't recall his name) was a good choice too! I remember he played the leading role in *28 Days Later*. He's an excellent choice. He's got that kinda face you expect a bad guy to have.Batman is not about special effects. OK, there are some very good action scenes, but Bruce Wayne's anger towards the thugs of Gotham and the one who killed his father is equally as important, maybe even more important.The human side of Bruce Wayne is what makes this movie so impressive. (And yeah, also that Batmobile and car chases :-) Bruce's not just some superhero that learns the bad guys a lesson. This Bruce has a personality, a history. Spider-Man has one too, but they haven't gone deeper into Peter Parker, they didn't go to the bottom of what he really is. I'm glad the writer(s) paid much attention to... how and why Bruce Wayne has become what he is now. I couldn't fall asleep last night, I just kept thinking how *wow!* this movie was. I haven't seen many summer movies this good, apart from Sin City. And gosh, it 's already in IMDb's top movies list! So that has to mean something to those of you who are still not sure whether or not they wanna see it in theaters or rent it. Very impressive movie. I rated it a 10. I never thought i would.

I was dubious before the screening of Batman Begins  I indeed felt the fear (coincidently this is the theme of the film) of disappointment. Schumacher's effort was as camp as a row of tents and relied heavily on Fx, silly gadgetry & overblown villains to wow and amaze us  sorry Mr Schumacher you failed miserably. Burton's world was better and his typical dark eeriness made the film enjoyable, but it still lacked the edge of the early Batman comics. Christopher Nolan's Batman Begins however has raised the bar so high even Spiderman with his fantastical web shooting powers couldn't swing over it. This film is surely now the benchmark we have to mark future comic book films by. Nolan's Gotham City is for want of a better word 'real', it could be any major city in the US and that's part of this film's huge appeal. The writing and plot are first-rate, I was relieved as my expectations of the writer who gave us XMEN and the Blade trilogy was very high  he hit the nail right on the head and knocked it in with a single blow. As for the bat himself played by Christian Bale  all I can say is he's truly tremendous in this role and is now the only person I could ever see in the infamous bat cape. He acts his socks off in this film and what a show he gives us  brooding, dry (watch out for the birthday party scene), injured as Bruce Wayne and then as his alter ego he rules - terrifying Gotham's villains as well as kicking the crap out of them. This is definitely Bale's film but the support of a stellar cast makes this film truly great. Liam Neeson, Cillian Murphy (excellent as the Scarecrow), Morgan Freeman, Gary Oldman & Michael Caine are fantastic is their roles. My only nit pick would be Katie Holmes never quite impresses as Bruce's childhood friend Rachel Dawes, don't get me wrong she is by no means below average (just see Pieces Of April for example) but it is hard to see her as a grown up Assistant DA  I blame Dawson's Creek Also Tom Wilkinson's crime lord character Carpone is a little too hammy for my liking, disappointing as he is one of the best British actors around at the moment However minor issues aside this is an excellent film for adults and teens alike  a word of warning for parents, the 12A certificate given in the UK is a little lenient in my opinion  some scenes (mainly the scarecrow fear scenes) are a little too much for the little 'uns. You have been warned! Overall rating *****

review: One of the best superhero movies made yet!
main_review: To start off with, let me say that I am not even a Batman fan. I am familiar with his character from cartoons and comics from when I was younger, but I never got into him as much as I did with heroes like Superman and Spider-Man. In fact Spidey is my favorite superhero. Which is why it is even more shocking to me that I liked Batman Begins more then any Spider-Man movie made yet.The acting in this movie is superb. Christian Bale is a perfect Bruce Wayne, and even though he sounds weird in his "Batman voice" he still great. Michael Caine portrays Alfred exactly as I imagined him, as does Gary Oldman with Jim Gordan. Murphy is creepy and convincing as Dr. Jonathon Crane AKA the Scarecrow. Ra's Al Ghul is also done excellently. Katie Holmes has a role that isn't needed, but plays it well none the less. Solid job all around.The action in Batman is great. There are no smiles on Batman's face like in "Batman and Robin," he attacks using intimidation and darkness...exactly how I imagined him. Great vision.And then we get to the most important part of the movie...the story. I really enjoyed how Nolan didn't start the movie with Wayne as a child, instead using those scenes as flashbacks. The story also benefits from not forcing two villains into a movie, but rather flowing them into the plot very well. Unlike the two more recent Bat flicks, Ra's and Scarecrow seem realistic and both feel like they belong fighting against Batman. And the semi-cliff hanger ending was great. I won't ruin it but Batman fans, even non-Batman fans, will all enjoy the reference made. I even enjoyed how much attention to detail there was in creating the Batsuit. Great job.On a side note the Batmobile is seriously the sweetest thing I have ever seen. When I first saw it I was expecting the worst, but now that I have seen it in action I cannot imagine Bruce driving anything else.Overall I am not just giving this movie a 10 because I am a crazed Batman fan...because I am not. But this movie proved all my doubts wrong and produced one of the best superhero movies ever made yet. If you haven't seen it go watch it. If you have seen it, go see it again...you may not have realized how good of a movie this flick really is.
