review: WOW! This is how it is supposed to be!
After 40 Years as a Fan,  I Finally Know Batman
main_review: Forty years ago, when reading the DC Comic and watching the TV Show, I would always be consumed by the questions..."Who helped build the Batcave? How did he make the utility belt? Who taught him how to fight?Finally, my Batman mysteries are spectacularly solved in the most stunning film adaption of any comic book ever. Batman Begins puts many mysteries to rest and provides the viewer with new ones. It is the smartest and most brutally touching Batman movie and has forced me to reevaluate everything that has been done with the hero to date.While I previously acknowledged the first Batman to be ground breaking, it is now 15 years later and Christopher Nolan seems poised to be the name that will be associated with Batman in film lore. His take on The Dark Knight is so powerful and emotional, it had me in awe of the action and near tears from the trauma that is Bruce Wayne's life.Burton's Gotham was a dark futuristic metropolis; Nolan, on the other hand, has created a city that is timeless, mixing the futuristic elevated transportation system with shadowy backgrounds that make you think of eras past. It is a setting and backdrop that will help this Batman's story be every bit as relevant in fifteen years as it is today. And what a story it is! Powerfully written to uncover more of the Batman's mask than any comic book or movie ever has, this is a movie that draws you in with brilliant characters, smart dialog and pure heart. And just as it has you in its emotional grasp, the action becomes intense. Fast and blinding, and very tightly shot, we never know where and how the Batman is attacking and this contributes to the mystery.As for Christian Bale, he is Batman and this is his movie. Looking back at the first two Burton efforts (which I still love in a now different way) I realize that they belonged to Nicholson's Joker and Devito's Penguin. Nolan has the confidence not to be seduced by comic book characterizations of villains to drive this movie. By using non- costumed heroes, he makes them more real and more frightening then the earlier versions. Liam Neeson's Ducard is more complex than earlier villains and his intense knowledge of Batman's history and psychology makes him especially intriguing.The rest of the cast is top rate, especially Gary Oldman as a surprisingly sedate pre-commissioner Gordon and Michael Caine as Alfred. The latter's relationship with Bruce Wayne was heartening and lent appropriate humor that never detracted from the tone of the film. I originally thought Katie Holmes was a little too bland for Bruce's love interest, but her final scene with Bruce revealed much depth to their relationship and it was wise to have the female lead be understated.In reading my comments, I don't want to be disrespectful to Keaton's Caped Crusader or Burton's directing efforts, but just as Tim Burton is rediscovering and reinventing an icon in Willie Wonka this summer, so too are Christopher Nolan and Christian Bales in Batman. And just as nothing will ever replace Adam West's campy Batman for me, I will still continue to watch the first two Burton Batman movies whenever they appear on cable, being amazed at their wit, action, and style. I don't think the jump could have been made from Bat-TV to Batman begins. There was a tremondous role for Burotn's Batman and it paved the way for a new genre. But Batman Begins peels the onion that is Batman in a different way still and this will be the one that forever touches my heart.

review: What a breath of fresh air.
main_review: Personally, this has been one of the most anticipated movies(along with AVP=( and x-men=) in my life, especially since that crappy Batman and Robin installment... Now I love Tim Burton's original Batman, but the problem was that Jack Nicholson stole the show (that's not a bad thing, but Batman's origins weren't dabbed into that much). The complete opposite is true with this movie- Ra's Al Ghul, the Scarecrow, and Carmine Falcone serve as great villains, but they all play second, third, and fourth fiddle to Bruce Wayne/Batman. And I am happy to say this movie was excellent; not just as a comic book superhero movie, but even as a standalone movie- everything was great, the music, the special effects(I love how an overbearing amount of CG was not used), the gadgets, the explanations, the story line, the beginnings of a legend. What a fantastic experience this was. This movie was all about Bruce Wayne and his transformation into Batman. Nolan did an excellent job of developing the characters and setting up for future confrontations with "other" villains. Also, Gary Oldman is great in this movie, as he is in most films that he does(notably Leon). Please, go see the movie. As a Batman film, it was dark and gloomy, just how a Batman film should be. I loved it.I will admit,the only detractor from the movie for me was Bale's voice as Batman (see the movie and you'll hear what I'm talking about), it was borderline corny, but I understand why he spoke like that.

review: Batman...the way it was meant to be
main_review: OK, let me just preface this by saying that I have been waiting for this movie for years. Ever since the debacle that was "Batman and Robin," I wanted to see Warner Brothers go back and get Batman right. Having waited so long, I was worried that, when the time finally came, I was bound to be disappointed. Fortunately, I was not. Not only has Batman been brought back to respectability, but it has exceeded the Tim Burton films by a mile. While they may have been entertaining flicks, one has to admit the first two Batman films, or any Batman film for that matter, was never about Batman. They were always about the villains, and it always made me feel somewhat shortchanged. Psychologically, Batman is the most interesting superhero around and none of the films ever got what he was all about. "Batman Begins" turns that all around and gets everything right that all the other movies got wrong. Batman/Bruce Wayne is finally that tortured and confused individual he was always meant to be: a borderline psychotic, only one step away from going down the path of the criminals he battles. Overall, the acting is first rate, the story is excellent, the direction is slick and the action is exhilarating. The only downside of this movie is the fact that now I have to wait another few years for the next installment.

I saw this film on a special staff preview as I simply could wait the extra 12 hours as I am a huge superhero fan on all levels, from Spiderman to Smallville.I was slightly sceptical about this film in the beginning because the last batman had seriously rocked my foundations of support. The action comes at you from all directions and it isn't just mindless fighting, its carefully choreographed martial arts which you would more expect to see in a matrix film.It wasn't until I came on here to spread the word of amazement, after calling my friends, that I read that it was an incredible 2 hours 40 minutes. Batman BeginsDir. Christopher Nolan Starring: Christian Bale, Katie Holmes, Michael Caine, Morgan Freeman, Liam Neeson, Gary Oldman, Tom Wilkinson, Ken Watanabe, Rutger Hauer and Cillian Murphy Rating: PG-13 for intense action violence, disturbing images and some thematic elements. Length: 141 minutes Rating: ****1/2 (Four and a half stars out of five)In the summer of 1989 history was made as director Tim Burton transformed one of the most popular comics of all time into one of the most popular films of the time, unleashing a dark and epic blockbuster that helped define a style. A franchise was begun, and its name was Batman.Then, in the summer of 1997 history was again made. Batman & Robin opened, a film that achieved the rare feat of almost single-handedly stopping a hit franchise dead in its tracks. To some it is even considered to be one of the worst mainstream films of all time, and such claims are not without merit. Boy did Batman & Robin kill, bury and then utterly destroy and blast into oblivion whatever respect the name "Batman" carried, at least when it came to the silver screen. So is it even possible, or reasonable, to bring back a franchise many would consider best left dead?Well, with a film as good as Batman Begins it is.Perhaps the best of the bunch in the recent explosion of comic book movies, the first thing that Batman Begins has going for it is the talent. Loaded with big names, from director Christopher Nolan (the man behind Memento, the 2000 indie hit that messed with time and psychology) to a cast featuring just about everybody on the planet, everything bristles with energy, veracity and most importantly purpose.Still, it takes more than big names to make a film good. There are no worries, though, as director Nolan is able to take all the money and opportunity thrown at him and mold potential into perfection. Or close to it, at least. Although a summer "event" film, there is much depth to be found amongst the explosions and car chases, and the film carries an emotional weight that few blockbusters care to bother with.Now, besides the luggage Batman Begins carries in the world of Hollywood, it also has a lot to explain when it comes to the events in a little place called Gotham. Several villains, including Scarecrow and Ra's Al Ghul populate this new Gotham, which itself no longer appears either goth or camp. Rather, Nolan's Gotham most resembles a real city.Then there's more characters in the form of a love interest played by Katie Holmes (don't tell Tom Cruise), and all the usual suspects such as the butler Alfred and the tech-guru Lucius Fox. Adding to an already full plate is a host of corrupt executives and seedy crime lords. And then of course there's Christian Bale as Bruce Wayne, or is it Batman? And make no mistake, this is his film.So yes, no doubt about it, Batman Begins is a busy film. Yet it never becomes a chore. Despite all the different characters and themes, the film enjoys connecting all the dots, and rather than breezing through the exposition to get to the good stuff it takes its time.Of course, the "good stuff" is still there. Namely, action! And of course the action does not disappoint. Not overused and always purposeful, i.e. never action for actions sake, it help keeps the film on the right track, towards class and not camp.Ultimately, though, this is a film that really isn't just about derailed trains and twirling police cars, and it is this determination to do more than offer pleasant eye candy that helps Batman Begins avoid the disposable nature of many films in its class (for an example just move over to the next theatre where Mr. and Mrs. Smith is likely playing.) This Batman is about the characters and what drives them, with most of them fleshed out beyond the simple black and white stereotypes of "good" and "evil." The only main complaint that jumps out comes near the end, where it seems a scene is completely left out. Part of downtown Gotham is in ruins, many are most likely dead or at least injured, and yet hardly any mention of this is made after the fact. However, it's a small nitpick, and Batman Begins ends on the same high-note it began with. As a sequel is hinted at, likely to feature Batman's most famous foe, a surprisingly high amount of anticipation is created as it becomes clear that the last words likely to go through the minds of moviegoers all about will be, "chill out."

As the movie started, I commented to my friend "please let this be great." And it surely was. Nolan does an amazing job in bringing the franchise back into focus and gives us hope of a bright future for Batman. The casting is incredible (although Katie Holmes is a little weak in her role). Michael Caine and Christian Bale have such a strong rapport together on screen. The way they bring Alfred and Bruce to life is what pulls the Bruce Wayne story fully together. Christian Bale is far and away the best fit of any actor to play the Batman role (yes -even better then Keaton). He shows everything - wit, menace, charm, rage and I look forward to seeing what he brings to the characters in the future. And the ending is very strong in terms of where you hope to see the characters moving forward and that not all is saved in Gotham. I pray for future Nolan Batmans starting now and whatever you do - go see this movie.

Going in to the theatre, I was rather skeptic about the quality of the performance that I was about to see, however I have to say that the Batman series has made a comeback that is absolutely unsurpassed. For those of you expecting to see another Batman and Robin: tough luck. This is a quality production, which although not quite in the tone of the previous ones, is still a masterpiece. It starts out a little bit rickety with childhood and adolescence scenes, but believe me these are very necessary for the plot. The essential story line is like this: during the time when Bruce's parents are killed, Gotham city is in a horrible depression and although his parents are attempting to fix this, they are not capable to do much. They are then killed by robbers as we all saw in the original Batman except with a few tiny changes, which really aren't that important. Bruce grows up a sad, depressed boy who is forever brooding about his parents' death. After a bit, when he is perhaps 20some he leaves do understand the dark mind of a criminal, already brooding the revenge of his parents. He encounters an organization that trains him and then attempts to use him to destroy Gotham City. He has a little bit of a conflict with them (to put it lightly) and then goes home to begin his fight against crime. What he doesn't realize is that the worst is yet to come.

'Bout damn time! As expected from a film with the word "begins" in its title, Batman Begins attempts to reset the Batman film franchise, effectively ignoring all the previous Batman films. Nolan and his crew perform this task perfectly. Not wasting a moment, the film opens with the newly launched DC logo then fades directly into a dark Warner Bros shield, which promptly explodes into thousands of bats. With this simple 10-second moment, the mood of the film is set. Billionaire Bruce Wayne's past is told in a series of flashbacks while being trained in the far off corners of Asian by the enigmatic Ducard (played perfectly by Liam Neeson) and long time Batvillain Ras Al Ghul (played by the talented Ken Wanatabe). For the first time ever in a Batman film we see that Bruce's parents are loving and caring individuals that not only love their son without question, but also deeply and truly wish to make Gotham City a better place for all its citizens. As such, the pivotal moment in Crime Alley is all the more terrible. Even though I knew the moment was coming, I still found myself cringing during the deadly mugging of Thomas and Martha Wayne. Nolan did an amazing job in creating real fear and pain in a scene that I have read literally thousands of times over. In fact, Nolan's direction through the entire film creates the greatest rendition of the Dark Knight ever put to the screen, small or large.Bale takes on the daunting task of creating a believable Bruce Wayne and Batman, a task he performs stunningly well. I have often stated that the only way to make Batman succeed is to have a perfectly acted Bruce Wayne, for he is the true mask. Bale is without a doubt the greatest Bruce Wayne. He is, at any given moment, the aloof billionaire playboy only to switch gears into the dark shadows of a man still wracked with pain and anger at the loss of his parents; as Batman, Nolan is able to channel his terror only before seen in American Psycho. There are moments in the film where the audience is truly intimidated by Batman. I would even go so far as to say that I found myself feeling sorry for the crooks of Gotham, when I wasn't clapping or grinning like a mad fan-boy. Michael Caine brings much needed depth and life to the character of Alfred Pennyworth. Ever more so then Bruce Wayne's butler, Alfred is the father figure that Bruce long ago lost in the bowels of Gotham, although he never over steps his bounds. Caine perfectly captures the wry humor that keeps an ever deeply brooding Bruce Wayne grounded. Rounding out this stellar cast is Gary Oldman as Sgt. Gordon who does a wonderful job of bringing Gotham's only good cop to honest life and I am deeply looking forward to more Gordon in future Batman films. Morgan Freeman as the business and tech savvy Luscious Fox, an old friend of Thomas Wayne and the man who holds the ideals of Wayne Enterprises long after his friend passed on. Cillian Murphy brings just enough analytical arrogance and flat out insanity to the part of Jonathan Crane, also known as the Scarecrow. Murphy perfectly plays a man barely hanging onto his own sanity. A man who takes true visceral pleasure out of the fear of others. Liam Neeson perfectly plays Ducard, a man who sees a potential protégé in Bruce Wayne. Neeson is able to take the now familiar role of wizened adviser and make it something completely different, even a tad sinister. I even found myself pleasantly surprised by the acting of Katie Holmes in the role of Rachael Dawson, assistant D.A. in Gotham City. While I don't completely feel her role was needed, it was not distracting and Katie's character is so much more then eye candy, unlike her predecessors in Kim Basinger or Nicole Kidman. Speaking of Gotham City, it is wonderful to see a Gotham that looks like an actual city. While I loved the work that Anton Furst did in Burton's Batman, it always felt like style over substance. Nolan's Gotham is real. She is a city that is alive, if sick and slowly dying from within. The Gotham City of Batman Begins is the city I had always envisioned Gotham to look (although I was hoping for a couple of GCPD blimps, maybe in the next film).I have often stated that films like Spiderman 2, Superman, and Hellboy worked because they weren't afraid to be a comic book films. That acknowledging the comic book world in which these stories reside is the only way such films can work. Batman Begins breaks that mold. True, Batman is a comic book character. True that Gotham City is a fake city in a fake world. However, Batman Begins is not a comic book movie. No, Batman Begins is a deeply moving and engrossing action / drama film that just so happens to draw its inspiration from a 66-year-old comic book icon. Batman Begins has some flaws, no that is not true, Batman Begins has some minor quips, but that doesn't stop me from claiming here and now that Batman Begins is the BEST comic book film yet made and quite possibly one of the best films of 2005 5 out of 5 critical hits.

FINALLY!!! A comic book movie that gets the essence of it's character right. FINALLY!! A Batman movie that gets the essence of the character right.I want to keep this review somewhat short because this film literally left me mouth agape and speechless. And yes in a good way. review: Bravo!  Quite simply: the best action-hero film ever.
main_review: Writer/Director Christopher Nolan has finally given Batman the respect he deserves. While the previous franchise films have been humorously entertaining at best, it is only with BATMAN BEGINS that are we treated to a hero with dignity and class.The casting choice of Christian Bale as Batman/Bruce Wayne was superb. His dashing good looks are secondary to his talent and depth, which is the true earmark of a bona fide actor. There hasn't been, nor is there currently, any other well-known actor that possesses the versatility, intelligence, charisma, and scintillating power, which Christian Bale possesses. The credit for bringing Christopher Nolan's vision of the Batman character to life *belongs* to him.Add the fine casting choices of Michael Caine, Liam Neeson, Morgan Freeman and Gary Oldman, and Mr. Nolan has set the scene for an astounding cinematic feast for **the heart**. Additionally, I suspect newcomer Gus Lewis, as the 8-year-old Bruce, will prove to be quite a talent in the years to come. They were all just brilliant.BATMAN BEGINS doesn't just entertain, it makes one *believe*.It will make you cheer, applaud, cry, laugh, and it will take your breath away!Encore! Encore! Encore!

Now, I'm no Batman expert, but I do know that the tale of him is supposed to be dark and serious. And if I'm correct, this movie certainly succeeded at emulating that feel. Sure, it isn't Star Wars Episode III, and the first Batman movies were certainly more fun (Batman Returns is still my favorite), although this movie probably was the first to accurately translate Batman to the big screen. Living up to my expectations from the trailers, I certainly recommend it to Batman fans.All in all, I give it a B. The movie ain't no Spider-man, but it was certainly no Hulk either (half exciting, half boring as hell). Christian Bale is definitely the Batman.

'Batman Begins" at last penetrates to the dark and troubled depths of the Batman legend, creating a superhero who, if not plausible, is at least persuasive as a man driven to dress like a bat and become a vigilante. The movie doesn't simply supply Batman's beginnings in the tradition of a comic book origin story, but explores the tortured path that led Bruce Wayne from a parentless childhood to a friendless adult existence.The story of why he identifies with bats (childhood trauma) and hates evildoers (he saw his parents killed by a mugger) has been referred to many times in the various incarnations of the Batman legend, including four previous films. This time, it is given weight and depth. Wayne discovers in Gotham that the family Wayne Corp. is run by a venal corporate monster (Rutger Hauer), but that in its depths labors the almost forgotten scientific genius Lucius Fox (Morgan Freeman), who understands Wayne wants to fight crime and offers him the weaponry.

After decades of trying, and even a worthy effort from Tim Burton, Nolan and crew have nailed the Batman. Choosing to focus on the motivation behind the character, putting aside the "cheesy" dialogue, they have created a Batman that truly would strike the heart of fear in the criminal element.I love that in this first installment they have chosen some of the more obscure Batman villains, leaving characters like the Joker, Riddler, etc. for future films. This allowed us to learn more about the history of the character.Major kudos to Bale who nails both ends of the character. He has the smug playboy nature of Bruce Wayne down pat (which shouldn't be a surprise after seeing him in American Psycho), but he also bring the intensity to the man behind the mask. In this film Bale has established himself as the quintessential Batman.This is a superhero movie for the ages!

review: Top Films of the Year... and The Year's Not Even Done Yet!
main_review: i don't like to give 10's to movies usually because to say so would say it is a perfect movie with no faults. NO movie has a perfect slate. This movie is definitely better than the two before it. However tends to go off on a tangent at times. The movie also tends to become a bit of a drag. The second half is where the fun really is. All characters give a decent enough performance. However it is the support team comprised of Caine, Freeman and Neeson that elevates this movie. Michael Caine as the good old butler is impeccable and plays his role perfectly. Morgan Freeman is Lucius a tech expert at Wayne enterprise who provides batman his cool gadgets. Liam Neeson plays Docard the leader of a ninja gang in the east. Christian Bale in the title role as batman is so so, I have seen better performance out of this talented actor. The action is as expected dark and very believable and Nolan gives his own touch (a big improvement over Joel Schumacher) to the movie. The visuals especially those shot in the Himalayas are breathtaking. All said "Batman Begins" is a new beginning after the two earlier fiascos.

This was one of those rare times where I left the movie theater in awe of what I had just seen. There were some lines/scenes in the movie that were incredible and Christian Bale does an unbelievable job. This is the best comic book movie ever and I am a huge fan of both Spider-mans so it was hard for me to say that. All the secondary actors (Freeman, Holmes, Neeson, Caine) did a great job as well. This movie was definitely worth the price of admission and I will probably be seeing it again in the near future

The best part of this movie is they finally got the correct casting for Batman this time. They finally chose Christian Bale the man who played "American Psycho" and another Orwell kind of movie, "Equilibrium".It makes me think they finally got it right for once! Val Kilmer looks like a comedian rather than Batman, George Clooney looked too cool to be a Batman, and others who played the role just doesn't have that chemistry. Michael Keaton as Batman looks too coward and not dark enough and not even close to being athletic.This is the first in a series that finally concentrate on Batman as the real actor instead of the villain. There were many twists and surprises in the casting and this added a great dimension. I mean Morgan Freeman who played Seven, is great in dark horror movie films that required serious tone, while Liam Neeson played well from his Star Wars Episode I. The big surprise that was Gary Oldman playing the good guy for once, really difficult viewing him because you are so use to him playing "Dracula" or some guy to destroy earth in the movie "The Fifth Element". Go this Oldman, I don't know if I should cheer him or be careful of him. He is the nervous element in the movie.The movie is somewhat good in tone, but could have improved on the theme of "Big Brother", which is a big serious topic in the internet world of New World Order. So the crime scene, the Mafia thing is a bit overdone, but I can take it. The fight sequences were too dark and could not see who is fighting who. The beginning sequences was sloppily done somewhat and the story was a bit too broken with flashback while he is training in the Himalayans. Because of some touches in the movie to New World Order, it would not be surprising that the mainstream media won't like the movie anyway, but most viewers will.Other than this the movie has a great display of realism and special effects was done well enough to believe that it was real enough for the general viewing. The psycho element and realism of Batman is done better than all the previous Batman because all the previous ones were over-the-top.The terrorism of destroying Gotham just doesn't add as to the realism of motive. Most motives in reality is that terrorism is either state- sponsored or a major corporation or consortium is behind the economic gains rather than some wild-eyed crazy religious (or philosophy) as this movie would indicate. Well, who am I to blame? Newspapers been doing that all the time and blaming on the patsy like Lee Harvey Oswald.However, it would have been much more realistic if economic gains were behind the destroying Gotham. An example is the series of James Bond 007 such as the movie Goldfinger.The writers did a good job however in showing the Wayne Enterprises' President were somehow behind the entire "terrorist act". Yes, you need TONS of money to finance terrorism and only corporate or state funding is needed for this kind of scale of terrorism.It is somehow eerily portrayed to remind you that the World Trade Center, as the train goes to hit the Wayne Enterprise building for a massive blow up of the city's water supply center. The writing could have been much more interesting if there were a clearer tie up to the President of Wayne Enterprise to be behind the entire fiasco and corruption that Batman and the owner of Wayne Enterprises tries to defend. However, this is the best Batman movie I have ever watched and I can stand the slow and choppy beginning and this can be overlooked on the strength of Christian Bale, Liam Neeson, Morgan Freeman, and Gary Oldman. I do not like the casting of Rachel, she looks like a child to play the part, but this again can be overlooked. Near perfect movie 10/10.

review: Best action movie since...I don't know...ever?
main_review: First off, I am not a gigantic fanboy of Batman. I thought the first one was pretty cool, and the rest got more and more disappointing. However, when I heard that Christopher Nolan was directing Begins, and Christian Bale was Bruce, I began getting excited. I went to the preview showing at midnight, and although I am extremely tired today, it was worth it.This is my favorite action movie since the LOTR movies. If you don't count those, it might be my #1 all time. The storyline was captivating, the villains menacing, the action gritty and raw. This movie delves into the psychology of his driving forces. The main theme, fear, is extremely well followed throughout the movie.This Batman is not a simple character who executes cool fight sequences. Has the look, the tone, the voice... could be a great choice.Any other ideas?

review: The best comic-book movie ever made
main_review: Batman Begins is the best comic-book movie ever made. Intelligently written, action-packed, yet with a surprising number of talking-heads scenes that make us care about the pyrotechnics later. But those pyrotechnics are not all CGI effects so much as they are feats of daring on a human scale. And that's what makes Batman Begins so winning.Since Batman is a mortal, a superhero without superpowers, the enemies are human too; no gimmicky Joker or Penguin, et al; no witty Gene Hackman in Superman, but scary Liam Neeson in a strong physical role. Ten-year-olds will be bored; this is a comic book movie for grown-ups, and it finally works. And with this movie, Christian Bale becomes a household name, he's that good (and looks great!).Highest praises to Christopher Nolan and the creative team that brought this artwork to fruition. By stripping away the visual gimmicks in earlier Batman films, we're left with a protagonist in whom we can personally relate.

Forget about the Luke-warm Episode III; a movie franchise that didn't succeed it's predecessors by sticking to the all-CGI method. I liked Yoda better as a puppet anyway. Mr. Lucas gave us a great trilogy with Episodes 4 - 6; and that's the way it should of stayed. Now we have a new hero to film saga film making, Christopher Nolan. He has created the first of what I see to be many new Batman pictures. Batman Begins is a wonderful film experience. The original with Michael Keaton was an excellent movie, but this film surpasses any and all expectations of fans of the original two; I say original two because I'm trying to forget about the Schumacher additions. Batman Begins is a much darker, in depth film. And it will be very, very hard for viewers to find flaws in any aspect of it both as a stand alone picture, and when compared to the Star Wars trilogy.

review: BEST FILM OF 2005, Tops my top 5 list now.
main_review: I was lucky enough to attend the midnight showing of Batman Begins, and from walking away from it, I have to say "wow". Words can't describe how beautiful of a film this is, for in the land of superhero movies, it not only blows away the Spiderman series, but practically every superhero movie that I've grown up with. This is the best Superhero film ever made.But maybe saying Superhero is a little off. Batman's more of a vigilante then a superhero. Sure it's a comic book superhero movie all around, but don't get me wrong, this is not a film you want to take the young ones too. It's dark, it's violent at times, and it's very moody. There's a lot of thematic elements in this film, including how Bruce Wayne deals with the death of his parents.The film opens with Bruce Wayne (played by Christain Bale) in a prison. He's there not because he's necessarily done anything wrong, but because he's studying the criminal mind. He's in a foreign country that is never explained, but it doesn't need to be explained. After getting in a street brawl with six goons at the prison, he's thrown in a solitary confinement cell, where Henry Ducard (Liam Neeson) begins to talk to him, telling him that he can train him.The first hour of the film is about the events that lead up to Bruce Wayne becoming Batman. They explain how he got the toys, what he's going to do, and why he's doing it.The real stand out role here isn't of Christian Bale as Bruce Wayne, but as Batman. The first night he goes out as Batman is probably the biggest and greatest scene I've seen in a movie. I love Michael Keaton, but Bale just blows him away in this performance. He even has the different voice down.There's a major plot twist at the end of the movie, and unless your a Batman junkie like myself, you will probably be surprised.Cillian Murphy does a fantastic job as Dr. Jonathan "The Scarecrow" Crane. Although he's not in the film a ridiculous amount of time, the film isn't centered on the villains, like the previous four films. It's also not outlandish, cartoonish, or down right stupid. None of the lines in the film were stupid to me, and the script felt like it was masterfully written.In fact the cast alone did a outstanding job. Even Katie Holmes (who plays Rachael Dawson) I thought did good, despite getting bad press for this film.The other real big stand out here though is Michael Cane. I love Michael Gough in the other four Batman films as Alfred, but Michael Cane just makes this so real, he's so caring and loving, you just love him.One other performance I'll mention is that of Gary Oldman who plays Sargent Jim Gorden. We all know later he's the Commishioner, but man he looks just like the comic books, and he speaks with the elegance you would expect of him. Outstanding.So will Batman Begins win any awards? I doubt it. Superhero films are snubbed year after year. But this year I really hope that the Academy has the imagination to look at some of the performances in this film, especially that of Christian Bale.Batman Begins easily goes down as not only the best super hero movie ever made, but one of the best films of 2005, if not, the BEST FILM OF 2005! I urge anyone to go see it.

I have a hard time giving comic book movies a perfect rating. Really, how can a comic movie be worth a 10? The answer is Batman Begins, a very faithful movie to the true Batman. Every single bit of info on how the Bat came to be is masterfully presented with slick cinematography and a powerful script. One of the surprising elements of the movie is how emotionally involved you become with Batman and Bruce Wayne. The action is intense and I have to say that the Batmobile is the best of any. I also saw this film on a Ultrascreen (what used to be an Imax theater) with powerful surround sound and thumping bass that makes the action that much better. The acting is superb (with special note to Michael Caine as Alfred... well done, old boy!) with powerful actors in several roles. Some might disagree with Katie Holmes as Rachel, but I found her to be an important and fitting role. One thing some people might have a hard time with is the surprisingly complex plot. A lot is going on in this movie outside of the rise of Batman. A second viewing may help to understand all that goes on may be required. (you will not mind seeing it again, I will see it as many times as I can) Fight sequences are nicely done and doing real stunts instead of CG goes a long way to giving Batman the right atmosphere. The CG that is used compliments the film and never overwhelms like in Star Wars. All in all, Batman Begins is the best comic movie ever made surpassing Spider-Man, Superman, and X-Men. The best part is that you do not have to be a fan boy to enjoy the movie. Ladies and gentlemen, rejoice, for Batman truly has returned!

review: I'm happy to finally be satisfied by a Batman flick
main_review: rating: 3 out of 4Director: Christopher Nolan Cast: Christian Bale, Michael Caine, Morgan Freeman, Katie Holmes, Liam Neeson, Ken Watanabe, Cillian Murphy, Tom Wilkinson Screenplay: Christopher Nolan, David S. Goyer MPAA Classification: PG-13 (intense action violence, disturbing images and some thematic elements)Batman has finally caught a break. Through five mediocre films the poor guy's stumbled around without even a superpower on his side. I mean, come on, Batman's just a buff guy in leather. He's one step above an S&M enthusiast. But now, with Batman Begins, ole' bat-ears has found his limelight. This film chronicles Bruce Wayne's (Christian Bale) rise to power in the New York copycat city Gotham to become the ever-popular Batman. We're brought through his rise from an East Asian prison to the mountaintop sanctuary, training with Ra's Al Ghul (Ken Watanabe) and Henry Ducard (Liam Neeson). There we're told of Bruce's childhood trauma that fuels his hatred for injustice. We're then spun along to Gotham City, where Bruce is looking to save the corrupt city from the clutches of the brutal mob boss, Carmine Falcone (Tom Wilkinson). But when Falcone's brought down on charges of drug smuggling, he pleads for insanity and actually wins. This brings Dr. Jonathan Crane (Cillian Murphy) into the picture. His examinations of numerous Falcone thugs have led to successful insanity pleas in Gotham's courtroom. Something smells fishy to Bruce. Or is that Batty? And with Rachel Dawes (Katie Holmes), assistant to the DA and childhood friend to Bruce, burrowing herself into danger with the Dr. Crane case, Batman's got his hands full. Much of Batman Begins success must be attributed to the brilliant star studded cast. I couldn't imagine a better actor behind the mask of Batman than Christian Bale. He brings an ideal mix of vengeance and humanity to a character that's hasn't felt quite right until now. Cillian Murphy as usual also does well. His role as Dr Crane/Scarecrow hits on the kind of evil bad guy that would usually be filled by such an actor as Jack Nicholson. And Morgan Freeman, Liam Neeson, Michael Caine, Ken Watanabe, Katie Holmes and Tom Wilkinson all fill in roles that, although are smaller than these caliber of actors are used to, play them as perfectly as humanly able. Director Christopher Nolan is most known for, as of right now, his work in Memento. The backwards time mystery masterpiece has been elevated to a kind of cult classic/critics choice. But now, almost undoubtedly, Nolan will be known as the man that made Batman work. The comic book hero has never looked so good. Most impressive is Nolan's work with his film's flawless atmosphere. Batman Begins is steeped to spilling point in atmosphere; with the perpetual nighttime, overtly common rain showers, and creepy dark alleys, this atmosphere is what brings Batman to a different level of Comic Book genre films than, oh say, Spiderman. Spiderman's world is a geek fanboy's dream. Sunshine spilling from a New York horizon with our nerdy hero staring off from his bedroom window to that of his first love across the street, enamored by the way the sun reflects off her golden blonde hairetc. Batman Begins plays an entirely different tune. This film is spectacularly dark. Gothic (no pun intended, by the way) is really the best way to describe it. We're presented with a man who's trained himself to embrace fear and use it against his enemies. Bruce Wayne is a guy that wants revenge on those that degraded his father's city to the dredges it is today. These grim overtones work to help flesh out what is quite a complex and surprisingly engaging storyline.There is, however, one very disappointing aspect of Batman Begins that I can't help but mention. In a comic book film we all know the best parts are going to be the action sequences. But here Batman, or rather Christopher Nolan, finally disappoints. The film resorts to cheap and overrated quick cuts that dizzy us into distraction instead of letting us actually witness the action. The fights become nonsensical and frankly boring when we're only allowed to glimpse half-second cuts at a time. This ruins much of what could be a very stimulating aspect of the film. Luckily, the rest of the film does not disappoint. Surprisingly, the most interesting aspect of Batman Begins is when it slows down to let us follow the story and look further into the world Nolan has so meticulously created. What I found interesting about the film's story is that it made an effort to incorporate more aspects of Gotham City than simply Batman vs. Baddie. We're presented with a tricky system of corrupt judges, cops, and lawyers; where all these are dealt with and strangely dissected using Rachel Dawes' sub-plot and an under-appreciated straight cop named James Gordon (Gary Oldman). We're also offered insight into Wayne Enterprises by way of Fox's (Morgan Freeman) sub-plot as the director of the Applied Sciences division where Bruce finds all his equipment. And lastly, the history and proud lineage of Bruce is played out by Michael Caine's character Alfred. In doing all this, Nolan looks beyond the simple comic book formula and succeeds in immersing us deeper into his Gotham City, making his crime trail storyline affect us more than we originally thought.I'm happy to finally be satisfied by a Batman flick. It's been a long time coming and with a few straggles aside, Batman's finally got something to look forward to.

review: Batman Begins is Off the Hook!
main_review: I realized in the wee hours this morning that Hollywood has been presenting us with more recycled, reused garbage than I ever allowed myself to see before. Batman Begins has opened my eyes. From the first few minutes of this film I was keenly aware that I was watching something completely original. The tone that Chris Nolan and cinematographer Wally Pfister have created for this movie is something entirely new to me. It is more epic feeling that Gladiator and drew me effortlessly into the depths of the film. Yes folks, it's true, I loved Batman Begins.I admit I am not an unbiased viewer. I wanted this movie to be brilliant more than anything in the world and damn it I knew it would be brilliant. I can however offer a distinct look from the Batman aficionado angle. As a girl who has a thorough appreciation for the intricacy and depth of the Batman comics I was grateful for the enormous effort made to create rich characters. Every character in this film has depth. It's simply stunning. On the other hand I can see how the average person who does not have a comic book background might ho-hum at this sort of movie. Some don't want to have to think and some don't want to have dynamic characters. Needless to say there is enough action here to satisfy even the basest viewer.Christian Bale steals the show. He is magnificentdare I say, Oscar-worthy? He seems to have a solid grasp of Bruce Wayne and his many personas and plays them all with fierce determination. The filmmakers were so confident in their choice that they often let the camera dwell upon him for lengthy moments so we can see his emotions and practically feel them as well. There are very few actors who are capable of such a feat (that would have been appropriate for the role). Some scene's left me giddy in my seat, swearing under my breath because I couldn't believe how utterly unhinged Bale was as the bat (Flass's interrogation comes to mind).And did I mention the score? While on it's own it feels a little disjointed, the score takes these brilliantly crafted moments and adds that buttercream frosting onto it. There is one particular scene in which Batman is in the Narrows facing Dr. Crane (involving a bit of fire) where the music is absolutely perfect. You feel like you're failing with Bruce when he does, you feel like you're angry when he is it's crazy good. It's all because of this excellent soundtrack.The supporting cast is unparalleled. They disappear into the story as if they've never starred in their own film before. It's amazing. Michael Caine's Alfred is probably my second favorite role after Bruce. He delivers a fantastic performance that wrenched my heart many a time. Gary Oldman was convincing and sympathetic. He is Gordon. Neeson so good. Even Katie Holmes did great and I knew she would surprise me. Even among all these great talents she did not stand out negatively. She blended in pretty well with the rest.The production design for this movie is going to win an Oscar. That's my prediction. Gotham looks stunning, sprawling real. Everything was real about this movie. I don't think I've ever been so drawn into a film before. My adrenaline was rushing so much I was able to drive through the night three hours back to my parents house in Eastern, MA. Whoa, man. Whoa. My heart thumped under my ribs throughout. I could not control my incredulous potty mouth. No movie has ever had this kind of effect on me.Before I saw Begins I'd already bought tickets to see the show three times this week. For good measure I'll be going a fourth time. Five stars dammit!

Got to take in the Midnight show of "Batman Begins" this evening with Ms. Addiction. Felt like writing up a little review, per the norm, so here we go.Batman is back with a vengeance. In what could quite possibly be the greatest casting in comic book movie history, virtual unknown, Christian Bale's performance single handily breathed new life back into the once downward spiraling super hero franchise. From the opening of the film, and the new DC Comics logo, I knew all in attendance were in for a treat."Batman Begins" serves as a prequel to the 1989 live action film that started it all, directed by Tim Burton. In "Begins", we're treated to a solid hour of Bruce Wayne's chronology and how the bat came to fruition. Introduced are Alfred (Michael Caine) as well as Wayne's parents via a series of flashbacks, cut in with present day episodes. These, a la "Godfather 2", clued viewers in to the origins and birth of the Dark Knight. Intense training montages between Bale and the always impressive Liam Neeson were just the beginning, dazzling to watch accompanied by the breathtaking landscapes.Act two weaves a story of how Wayne's once industrious hometown of Gotham City has become overrun by crime and violence, in desperate need of a heroic savior. Wayne, a supposed avid spelunker, stumbles upon a cave under his age old mansion, there, learning to embrace his fears, giving birth to his alter-ego, and thus finding motivation to save his hometown. Enter shady individuals like crime boss Falcone, and Jonathan Crane, aka "Scarecrow", brilliantly portrayed by "28 Days Later" star Cillian Murphy. Always looming in the background is Wayne's love interest, Rachel, played by Katie Holmes. While his guilt is outweighed by something else, Bale digs deep to take the law into his own hands, while exorcising his personal demons, ridding Gotham of the infestation.What surprised me most about the film was how it felt less like the colorful, flashy, quippy comic book films were so used to. Batman was indeed dark, back to the Burton way of things, Only this time, he's got the machismo, the cunning, and the inner anger that the character was so sorely lacking. Bale equals perfection, as I said. In addition, he was surrounded by absolute Grade A supporting talents. Morgan Freeman, Katie Holmes, Michael Caine, Ken Watanabe, Liam Neeson, Rutger Hauer, Gary Oldman! It's a dream cast, and it flowed like such. The collective was absolutely incredible. The films presentation was also very intriguing, giving Batman a complexity to go with the newly uncovered origins.My complaints are VERY few and far between, and lie mainly in chronology and continuity. If this were to serve as a prequel to the Burton original, there are flaws in the time line. In the original Batman, his parents were killed in 1922. Then in Burton's film, it was closer to 1955, then in "Begins", it had to be around 1997, as there was clearly a Black 1999 Oldsmobile Aurora at Wayne Manor for the funeral, meaning "Begins" was actually taking place closer to 2010-2015? This was never really cleared up. Also, if Chill killed Wayne's parents, was Jack Napier lying in Burton's "Batman"? Overall, I can say that this is easily the best cast comic book film of all time, and quite possibly the best Super Hero film I've ever seen. The adult theme worked, and was a welcome change. I'm glad to see Christopher Nolan resurrect the Bat, salvaging its dignity, with David Goyer's redeeming co-writing, after the atrocity that was "Blade: Trinity".9.5/10 Batarangs..

review: Best movie since 2000! Easily the best Comic Book movie EVER!

review: As of today...this is the greatest SuperHero movie ever created.
main_review: One word: AMAZING! Something that should be understood about this film first off, this is not a movie for young children. I'm a 32 year old man and there were parts in this film that scared the **** out of me. For the past six months I've waited for this film with a strong anticipation. My wife has been telling me for the past two months that I shouldn't get my hopes up because she didn't feel that this movie could live up to the hype that I had given it. Not only was she wrong but she went with me and can't stop talking about it. The acting is absolutely spot on. Every part was cast perfectly and without a doubt the greatest character is the caped crusader. I was thoroughly impressed with how much chemistry existed between ALL of the main characters. Who ever the casting director was for this film deserves a nice fat check for this one. Their work is impeccable. Not only was the acting wonderful but the writing is equally as impressive. The language was complex and intelligent but not over the top and confusing. There are many words of wisdom used in the film that any person could easily incorporate into their every day life. All in all this is truly one of the best movies that I've seen in quite some time. Forget Star Wars, The Smith's, and anything else that comes out this year, this is a true "must see movie." Kudos to all that were involved with this movie, you have truly made a film that will stand the test of time... thank you.

I'm not here to tell you the plot of this movie. A review should not do that. I'm not here to blast off about my opinion mindlessly. I am certainly not here to demand everyone like this film.I'm here to advise you, from one film-goer to another, that "Batman Begins" is officially worth your notice, comic book fan or no. Hollywood simply does not put out films like this very often.Christopher Nolan's epic Batman origin tale is very different from the other movies made about the Dark Knight. Unlike Joel Schumacher and (to an extent) Tim Burton, Nolan is not interested in Batman's toys or his neuroticism nearly as much as he's interested in the city at stake, the people inside of it, and most of all the man who wants to save both. Ironically, this focus on human drama makes the toys far cooler and the mystique far more legit, because the film never feels like it's leaning on them.Credit is owed to every single member of the cast, but some more than others. Christian Bale nails it, but the fans and the critics were pretty sure he was going to; he is the only man for this job. Morgan Freeman and Michael Caine have so much class and style it comes out of their ears. Liam Neeson, often jeered at for supposedly reprising his role as Qui-Gon Jinn here, actually constructs a vastly different type of tutor than his old Jedi master: a brutal, frightening, unforgiving man whose complex motives and dangerous beliefs are manifested perfectly throughout the film. He is as engaging as Bruce Wayne without ever upstaging him. We get the sense this man could have become Batman himself long ago, but did not. Also worth mentioning is Katie Holmes, who is getting collateral flak from fanboys displeased by her casting. Disregard such flak. She does a fine job, shaming Kim Basinger's helpless damsel and creating a real moral challenge for Bruce Wayne.The last time David S. Goyer took part in writing a movie, he constructed the unforgivably bad "Blade: Trinity." When I saw it, I became very concerned for this film. It is now clear that Goyer had to hit his career low before he could nail his high. Although he has done some very enjoyable work in the past, this is the best film David Goyer has ever had anything to do with. All of the "Blade" trilogy combined can't take this beast for raw power.Christopher Nolan, however, is still the man that ran this show, and had the vision for it in the beginning. As such, he is the man who deserves the biggest applause. He has succeeded in making a super-hero movie about something, a movie which completely succeeds in telling a rich, complicated story about what fear can do and how to overcome it. This theme is not subtle or passive, but actively influences every second of the movie, giving it incredible continuity and focus. Nolan gets the applause for that more than anyone else. It is his achievement that this film is so finely crafted; he was the beating heart of this animal, and he brought it to glorious life.Underestimate "Batman Begins" at your own peril.

review: a midnight ticket well worth it
Finally, something to talk about this summer
main_review: So I think we all have watched our fair-share of comic book movies in our day. Its not a surprise that some have succeeded and that some have failed. What we have here is a great example of just how good this type of film can be. I just walked out of the 12:01 showing of Batman Begins and I was blown away.What we have here is Christopher Nolan taking the Batman series and resurrecting it. Nolan has done a fantastic job in the past with both "Memento" and "Insomnia" and he's equally successful here. This is no little accomplishment; anyone who has seen the last few Batman films would agree that it is not difficult to make a bad film. Also to be taken into consideration, Nolan is telling the tale of how it began. Where others have had their Batman waiting to take flight, Nolan was forced to create his own. Onto the film. The beginning of the film focuses on creating Nolan's Batman. This part is heavy on the dialogue and light on the action. This works wonders because far too often we see directors avoiding the foundation that Nolan embraces here. We meet characters, villains, and our hero at this time. Without getting into too much detail, Bruce Wayne is away from Gotham for a portion of time to find himself. Once he succeeds, he returns to explore the city for what it has become.I'm trying my hardest to avoid detailing the plot, because it was too entertaining watching it develop before my eyes to reveal its fun. What I will tell you is this. The film is dark, very dark. This may be hard to believe, but it is much darker than Burton's Batman, and thats saying something. Bale plays the role well, as does the rest of the cast. Pay particular attention to Cillian Murphy who outshines the rest. His portrayal of Dr. Crane was on target, to say the very least. Overall, Batman Begins is a huge success. The film allows for a plot to develop and does not rely on special effects. When CGI is used, its used to perfection (the railway running through Gotham is gorgeous). I would recommend the film to anyone for it requires little knowledge of the Batman series, and is overall a great film. The summer may actually be worth sweating through this year.

I just saw the movie and it rocks. This is by far the best of the Batman Movies. Even considering that it is 16 years since Batman 1 came out, this film serves the Batman franchise better than any before it. It's absolutely horrifying in some scenes, I'm surprised that it's only pg-13. Overall, every scene in the film, outside Wayne Manner, is gritty, intense and brilliant. I'm a HUGE Batman fan. I've read and over the years injested the darkest Batman stories told. Including The Dark Knight Returns and Batman Year 1. This film not only stays true to that vision of Batman, but expands upon it. Everyone from the Die Hard fan to the casual movie goer should be satisfied with this portrait of Bats/Wayne. The casting, the directing, the sets, the makeup, the wonderful toys, all make the viewer wanna go out and kill Paul Allen and forget about it 5 minutes later. This movie gets 2 Bat ears way up. SEE IT! If you can see it on IMAX!

Absolutely stunning.If I had a complaint it would echo one I have in a lot of action movies these days -- the sequences were shot in that contemporary quickjerk, post-matrix style that I find so annoying.You know, the style where its like the director just tosses the camera into the fight and all you see is like a whirling dervish. You cant even tell who is winning.In Batman Begin's case though, all is forgiven. Who needs George Lucas when you have Chistopher Nolan. He has painted the character of Batman as it should be. He has brought back all this was good in the original Batman movies (The first two) and then he made it his own. Christian Bale shines and the caped crusader and shows us who the dark night truly is. I hate to say much about the movie its self, because that is the beauty of this picture, you learn with every frame who Bruce Wayne is, was, and will be. This is by far the best Batman film made. I cannot explain what justice this does for the Batman franchise. review: The best Batman movie ever made...
main_review: FINALLY!!!! After Batman and Robin, I had all but given up on there ever being a great live-action Batman movie. Sure, the Burton ones weren't all that bad..but none reached the level of any of the animated shows. In fact, to date, the best Batman movie was 1993's animated Mask of the Phantasm.That is until I saw Batman Begins last night...this is a fantastic movie. It's intelligent, it's fun, a little scary, exciting and it's the best Batman movie ever made.Finally the debate as to "Who is the best Batman?" can finally be laid to rest. Christain Bale is terrific. With the exception of the animated voice-over work of Kevin Conroy, Bale is Batman, hands down. Watch for the scene where Batman dangles a dirty cop from the side of a building while he interrogates him ("SWEAR TO ME!!!")....the intensity in his eyes and the ferocity in his voice blows away anything from Keaton/Kilmer/Clooney era.The rest of the cast is all top notch, which is really no surprise considering the resumes of the talent involved. Best of all is Freeman who turns in a fun performance as Luicus Fox, the man who provides Batman with all his wonderful toys and Gary Oldman, playing a good guy for the second movie in a row (first Sirius Black, now this). Even Katie Holmes is good.David Goyer (who disappointed me with Blade 3) totally redeems himself with this script. He sets the mood just right. No puns, no silliness, just good stuff. It gets a little preachy in the beginning with Qui-Gon Neeson but by the second hour, it's all good.The only downsides to the movie are minor. BB follows the Spider-man template (no costume for the first hour), Ken Watanabe's part is really limited, the music is not as memorable as Danny Elfman and the fight scenes are a little too tightly shot.Other than that, this is well worth the $10 to see it. If you can see it in IMAX, all the better. Just bring your earplugs (it is LOUD) and enjoy.Go see this movie....NOW!

If you don't know who's in this movie, you'll get a kick out of having them pop up one by one, each more a kick in the butt than the previous. This is story driven, and it makes you wish that more Hollywood movies would take the fundamental importance of the story more seriously. It's always such a letdown to watch all the hollow, pointless explosions and such, and let's not forget that empty, horrible feeling you have leaving the theater knowing you've been had and that you just fed the machine your money. B.B. will not let you down. So sit back, relax, and enjoy the ride, safe in the belief that you won't be slinking quietly back out into the real world like a one night stand gone bad.

This is easily one of the best superhero origin stories and one of the best superhero movies in general. I actually prefer this to the year one comic origin, the fact they showcase some of batmans actual training and travels and give a tease on just how long and hard it was is really cool. The way all the pieces of this story fit together is also very well done and really makes a complete arc. Something not many people talk about with this movie, is that it doesn't play itself too seriously, characters will make jokes in a very realistic way that doesn't feel cheesy but instead natural and allows the movie to be much more enjoyable. All that being said I do have a couple issues with this film, my biggest is the action, the first action scene is really entertaining but after that I feel the movie relys way too much on jump cuts, causing very messy and confusing fight scenes where you can't really see what is happening. Like most origin stories, I did personally find that it did drag a little, considering the movie spends nearly half its runtime before he gets the suit it surprisingly doesn't drag as much as you'd think, but around the 40 minute mark I did find it dragging. Funnily enough though I'd actually say the Bruce Wayne side of this film is the most entertaining, Batman is amazing in this film don't get me wrong, but the bruce Wayne scenes actually might be more interesting. Another issue I have with this movie is scarecrow, I think he serves the plot perfectly but it does feel a little disappointing at just how underused he is. If I was to nitpick I also think Christian bales deep voice comes off a bit too goofy at times, this might just be from the memes but he deepens his voice so much at times that it almost feels like a parody, for the most part this isn't too distracting though, and I think a fair amount of the scenes that are, were meant to be comedic anyway. My final gripe with this film, is the ending fight does feel a little contradictive, it's not too big of a deal but I feel it was an incredibly weird choice for the film and it does slightly hurt the character arc and plot. Overall this is a great origin story that really understands exactly what Bruce Wayne is as a character, it has a fair amount of issues, but they all feel minor when the story is articulated so well.

Christopher Nolan's "Batman Begins" resurrects the iconic superhero from the depths of cinematic mediocrity, breathing new life into the beloved franchise. In this origin story, we witness the transformation of Bruce Wayne, portrayed with depth and conviction by Christian Bale, from a troubled heir to a symbol of justice and hope.Nolan's narrative unfolds like a tapestry, weaving together the threads of Wayne's past traumas, his training with the enigmatic League of Shadows, and his emergence as Gotham City's vigilante protector, Batman. The film delves into the psychological complexities of the character, exploring themes of fear, vengeance, and the blurred line between heroism and vigilantism.Technically, "Batman Begins" is a triumph. Nolan's direction is sleek and atmospheric, capturing the gritty realism of Gotham's urban decay while infusing the film with a sense of grandeur befitting its comic book origins. The action sequences are pulse-pounding and visceral, choreographed with precision and flair.The ensemble cast delivers stellar performances across the board. Bale brings a brooding intensity to the role of Bruce Wayne, while Michael Caine shines as the loyal butler Alfred Pennyworth. Liam Neeson exudes menace as the enigmatic Ra's al Ghul, and Cillian Murphy is chillingly effective as the sinister Scarecrow.One of the film's greatest strengths lies in its exploration of moral ambiguity. Nolan presents a nuanced portrayal of good and evil, challenging traditional notions of heroism and villainy. This complexity adds depth to the story, elevating "Batman Begins" above typical superhero fare.While the film occasionally stumbles in its pacing and exposition, these minor flaws are overshadowed by its overall impact. "Batman Begins" lays a solid foundation for Nolan's epic Dark Knight trilogy, setting the stage for deeper exploration of the Batman mythos in the films that follow.In conclusion, "Batman Begins" is a thrilling and thought-provoking reimagining of the Caped Crusader's origin story. With its rich character development, stunning visuals, and thematic depth, it stands as a testament to the enduring power of the Batman legend.

review: atman Begins: A Dark and Riveting Rebirth of the Caped Crusader
main_review: Rating: 9/10 The Dark knight is a better movie but this is a better Batman movie.Christopher Nolan's "Batman Begins" serves as a cinematic masterpiece that not only revitalizes the iconic superhero genre but also redefines the origin story of one of the most beloved comic book characters, Batman. With a perfect balance of gripping storytelling, stunning visuals, and exceptional performances, this film sets the stage for a new era in superhero cinema.Christian Bale delivers a stellar performance as Bruce Wayne, bringing depth and humanity to the character. His journey from a disillusioned and vengeful young man to the formidable Dark Knight is portrayed with raw emotion and conviction. The film's exploration of Bruce Wayne's internal struggles and personal demons adds layers to the character, elevating him beyond the typical superhero archetype.The supporting cast is equally impressive, with standout performances from Michael Caine as Alfred, Gary Oldman as Jim Gordon, and Liam Neeson as the enigmatic Henri Ducard. Each actor brings nuance to their roles, contributing to the film's overall sense of realism and gravitas.Nolan's direction is masterful, and his decision to ground the story in a more realistic and gritty world sets "Batman Begins" apart from its superhero counterparts. The dark and atmospheric cinematography, coupled with Hans Zimmer's haunting score, creates an immersive experience that keeps audiences on the edge of their seats.The film's narrative structure, expertly woven between present-day events and flashbacks, allows viewers to witness the evolution of Bruce Wayne into Batman. The exploration of fear as a powerful weapon and the philosophical themes of justice and morality add intellectual depth to the film, making it more than just a typical superhero action flick.The action sequences are intense and well-choreographed, showcasing Batman's martial arts prowess and gadgetry. Nolan's commitment to practical effects and minimal use of CGI adds a tangible and authentic feel to the film's visual spectacle.While "Batman Begins" serves as an origin story, it also lays the foundation for Nolan's celebrated "The Dark Knight" trilogy. The film's success in reimagining the Batman mythos and setting a new standard for superhero storytelling makes it a pivotal entry in the genre.In conclusion, "Batman Begins" is a triumph on multiple fronts - from its character development and performances to its atmospheric cinematography and thought-provoking themes. This focus on character development allows for a deeper understanding of Batman's motivations and establishes a strong foundation for the subsequent films in the trilogy.The screenplay, co-written by Christopher Nolan and David S. Goyer, strikes a perfect balance between action, drama, and philosophical themes. review: Rethinking Comics on the Big Screen
main_review: Tim Burton's successful films "Batman" and "Batman Returns", as well as their less notable sequels "Batman Forever" and "Batman and Robin" from Joel Schumacher set some tone for the narrative about probably the darkest widely known crime fighter in the DC universe. All the more vivid was the new reinterpretation of Batman under the leadership of Christopher Nolan. The director seems to have turned the world of comics upside down, demonstrating that fictional costumed heroes and villains can perfectly fit into the real human world."Batman: The Beginning" I have always somehow compared with the previous tetralogy. And Nolan's film, which originally existed in my understanding as a kind of prequel, was very different from these adaptations about the Gotham Knight. Nolan's world is a vibrant Gotham that existed in Bruce Wayne's youth, and then a metropolis mired in corruption and violence. Nolan perfectly demonstrates this change with light tones in flashback scenes, and also shows a dark and gloomy city at the time when an avenger in a bat mask appears in it.We are shown the path of becoming the main character, who was well shown by Christian Bale. Before this, we had not seen a full-fledged origin in the cinema. Therefore, the origin of Batman turned out to be very important, both from the point of view of the plot and in general for understanding the complex character of Wayne on the screen as a whole.The picture allows you to follow the formation of the hero through the demonstration of several significant figures from comics in this story at once. First of all, this is the butler of the Wayne couple, Alfred Pennyworth, who raised an orphan. Michael Caine is a great actor. All his roles are great, but the role of Alfred is special for me. He is a kind of father and senior companion for the main character, the kind of person who may be missed in his younger years by a seemingly grown-up guy. For paternal advice for a young man may well seem out of place, and an older authoritative friend who has been around all his life often does not happen in real life. And Alfred here acts as a kind of substitute for a parent and at the same time a wise adviser. Always witty and bright, but at the same time not oppressive and allowing Bruce to experience adult life himself.Another important character is James Gordon, played by the equally iconic actor Gary Oldman. The transformation of the actor into a positive and strong hero turned out great. If earlier for me he personified the villains from the "Fifth Element" or "Leon", then here he is a completely different person. A guardian of the law, a loving family man, a just man. Oldman is a great actor and his role as Gordon here is also important in the formation of Bruce Wayne.In the film, we are shown three villains from Batman comics at once. It was a bold move for its time, because, as a rule, the hero and the villain converge one on one. Nolan went further, showing the Scarecrow, Falcone, Ras al Ghul in the picture. Again, except for the saturation of the narrative and confrontations, I see such an introduction for Bruce Wayne to come to become Batman. After all, it was Carmine Falcone who opened the young man's eyes to what was happening in his hometown, forcing him to think about how Bruce could influence the situation, being the "prince of Gotham", a billionaire who simply lives his life aimlessly. The scarecrow becomes the personification of fear. Bruce decides that it is with the help of fear suggestion that he will fight criminals, thereby creating a kind of sword of Damocles - criminals will always be afraid to do something illegal, because Batman is somewhere, and he will definitely come for them. Well, Ras al Ghul, the man who taught Wayne, gave him knowledge about controlling himself and his fears. Batman takes something from everyone. And collectively becomes the one who will later be called a Legend.Visual and audio rows are pleasing. The production is excellent, the battle scenes are beautiful, the music is beyond praise. Zimmer and Howard's soundtrack will definitely be remembered for their motives. The Oscar nomination for the best work of the operator is also an indicator of the quality of the project.Christopher Nolan's work is definitely worth a look. This is the beginning of an excellent trilogy, a film with a lot of interesting ideas, visual and technical solutions, a film that sets a new fashion for superheroics.9 out of 10.

review: "Your anger gives you great power. But if you let it, it will destroy you. As it almost did me"
main_review: The best phrase to describe Batman Begins would be a perfectly balanced classic'.This is a phenomenal superhero movie, and one of the best films that I have had the pleasure of watching.Batman Begins is a heavily character-driven story, but the beauty of it is that it manages to combine the perfect blend of action, drama, emotion, suspense, and beautifully crafted storytelling throughout the length of the feature.The origin of Batman was the right place to give the franchise a unique breadth of life, most people know of Bruce Wayne who turned to vengeance after the death of his parents. But this is the first time we see a confused, but intelligent, Bruce which takes him into the depths of the criminal underworld.In Batman Begins, Bruce Wayne is searching for his identity, he meets Henri Ducard while in a prison cell who informs him that they are fighting on the same side. Bruce then journeys onwards toward the league of shadows who are led by a man by the name of Ra's Al Ghul.Once at the Himalayan temple of the League Of Shadows, Bruce undergoes a grueling training regime to transform his body and mind into something more than a man, a symbol that can inspire hope and will put fear against those who would use fear themselves.In this story, you naturally forge an emotional bond with Bruce Wayne's transformation into Batman. You follow his struggles, and his actions against Gotham's criminal underbelly which is told with clever dialogue by Rachel Dawes, and then repeated back to her later in the film by Bruce Wayne thus revealing his identity 'It is not who I am underneath, but what I do that defines meThere is maybe only a handful of performers that speak with a commanding presence. One is Liam Nesson, and the other the Michael Caine. Every time one of them spoke they stole the scene. There is just an aura of white noise in the background so that you are silently alert, and you take notice of absolutely everything that they have to say.When a film becomes iconic such as Batman Begins, it's not just the epic storytelling, but also it's a lot to do with the dialogue or phrases that leave you with a powerful, lasting impression.Some of these imprint in your mind and stay with you forever such as a phrase from Bruce's father 'Why do we fall, Bruce? So we can learn to pick ourselves back up.The discussion between Alfred and Bruce 'Why bats, Master Wayne? Bats frighten me. It's time my enemies share my dread.And even Henri Ducard 'You must become more than just a man in the mind of your opponent'.Batman Begins has a monumental ensemble cast, one that is almost unrivaled in today's cinema. Christian Bale as Batman, Michael Caine as Alfred, Katie Holmes as Rachael Dawes, Cillian Murphy as Dr. Crane/Scarecrow, Gary Oldman as inspector James Gordon, Morgan Freeman as Lucius Fox, Tom Wilkinson as Carmine Falcone, Rutger Hauer as Earle, Ken Watanabe as Ra's Al Ghul and Liam Neeson as Henri Ducard.It's also worth noting that Director Christopher Nolan is extremely bold but adventurous. Many of the action sequences are done without CGI. He demands a certain level of realism which means everything you see represents our world in some way, and therefore he has a great sense of believability in his work.Batman Begins is exactly how you should tell a story with cinema. It transports you into the world and gives you a little bit of everything with a vast variety of locations, props, and characters to keep you feeling engaged and interested.Overall there was a wonderful collaboration in this picture. From the opening scenes in Iceland to the gritty Narrows, extensive cityscapes, and fine attention to every detail including the grueling fighting styles this is a film that will be remembered for the ages.9/10.

main_review:
For its genre, this is a nice comic-book film, though it waddles along with Hollowood's nefarious cliches and
CGI over story.Here's my breakdown:STORY:
Most know the general story here. Suffice to say this plays much deeper into Bruce Wayne's insatiable need
for vengeance. The difference here, vs the original with Keaton and Nicholson, is the opulence of scenery
and weapons technology. The question I always ask is: do the additions of context add to the story? The
answer here, as is usually the case, is "No."At some point in film-making, someone started to turn up the pace of visuals, and that required non-human
techniques ... enter Computer Generated Imagery(CGI). The sad part is that story and acting suffered in order
to produce impossible situations. Some argue that's satisfying desperate fans' addiction to greater sensory
stimuli. I argue that it ruins storytelling and the human brain.ACTING:
The acting here is OK, even with Bale, Caine, Freeman, Oldman and Neeson doing their best. My impression
is that everyone was corralled into the pit of an empty script and shallow characters. Thus, none of them were
free to express the characters in their own unique style. Dunno.ENTERTAINMENT:
Entertainment value probably depends on what you've become accustomed to. For many younger folk, this
probably has a high value. For a senior, like me, it leans moderate.TEMPO:
There are some meaningful and well-paced scenes and sections, but far too few. Most of this is ripping through
scene after scene, one liner after another. Too quick for actual storytelling.CINEMATOGRAPHY:
In parts it's gorgeous, but eventually devolves into explosions and endless "epic" music.DIRECTING / WRITING:

which was ditto on the messiness.Last, I'll just reiterate my old chime - don't write and direct.Writers: I thought Goyer did a good job with "Blade" (1998) and "Dark City" (1998), but the rest of his work seems
